This release's headline feature is a real magic point source picker: casting a spell now lets you choose where the points come from whenever more than one source is available. POW-storing crystals work as an alternate source instead of the old max-boosting hack, a Rune Priest's Allied Spirit can share Magic Points, Rune Points, and spell knowledge with its priest, spirits trapped in an item via a Binding Enchantment can be drawn on the same way, and a Spell Matrix Enchantment lets a Spirit Magic spell travel with a physical item for anyone holding it to cast. Magic Points and natural Hit Point healing also stop being something you have to track by hand: both now recover automatically as game time passes, computed straight from the world clock instead of a manual catch-up step. Alongside that, resolving a season's worth of pending Experience checks no longer means chasing across the Skills, Rune, and Passion tabs to find every one and opening a separate dialog for each. A new Experience Roll Session lists everything pending at once with an optional Roll All action. And a quadruped creature like a horse gets its own hit-location layout on the Combat tab now, instead of a default table layout.

#956 #1023 Any Gear, Weapon, or Armor item can now act as a POW-storing crystal. Open the item and set a value greater than 0 in the Stored Magic Points fields: the first represents how many points are currently stored, the second the maximum it can hold. The "Magic Points Identified?" checkbox is a gate the GM can use to hide from the players that the item is a POW-storage item. A storage item only counts as a usable source once it's both equipped and identified - equipped to match Core's "physical contact" requirement for a Magic Point Enchantment, identified so an unidentified crystal doesn't announce itself as a battery. Once a GM sets a max stored points value on the item, it joins the caster's own pool and any Allied Spirit bond as a possible Magic Point source. Which of those show up as sources at all, and in what order, is managed from a new Magic Point Source Order popout on the character sheet, with drag-and-drop reordering - the red numbers show that order. That popout also has a button to move Magic Points from the character (self) into the crystal, moving as many as it can without knocking the character unconscious. Casting a Spirit Magic spell (or boosting a Rune Magic spell with magic points) now shows a "Magic Point Source" dropdown. It defaults to "Auto," which drains through the sources in that popout's order - the caster's own pool is just one entry in that order - but you can also choose to draw from one specific source for that cast only, if you want. Every option other than "Auto" itself shows its current/max Magic Points directly, so you can tell at a glance which source actually has anything left before choosing. This replaces the old approach of bumping an actor's Magic Point max via an Active Effect on the item, which merged a crystal's points into the owner's own pool instead of keeping them as a separate, spendable reserve. Any item still using the old active effect approach is migrated automatically the next time your world runs its migrations - no manual cleanup needed. Manual cleanup needed if you tracked crystal charges via Quantity If you instead tracked a crystal's remaining points by hand using its Quantity field (e.g. Quantity 5 meaning 5 points left, decrementing it as points were spent), that pattern isn't covered by the automatic migration - there's nothing in the data for it to recognize. Set the item's new Stored Magic Points value/max yourself, then set Quantity back to 1 - and consider switching the item's type to Unique since you no longer need it to behave as a Consumable.
documents.s: Magic Point Storage and Source Picker

documents.t: #957 #1002 A Rune Priest's Allied Spirit is now more than flavor text. Link the bond partner from the priest's Combat tab in edit mode by dragging the spirit actor to the Allied Spirit dropzone. From then on - in either direction - the pair share Magic Points, Rune Points for any cult they're both initiated to, and known Spirit Magic and Rune Magic spells. That means a priest can cast a spell their Allied Spirit knows (or vice versa) by drawing on the other's points, even for spells they never personally learned - shown on the caster's own Spirit/Rune Magic tab under an "Allied Spirit:" divider so it's clear the knowledge isn't really theirs. Shared Magic Points also get their own entry in the Magic Point Source Order popout, marked with a spirit rune so you can tell an Allied (or bound) Spirit apart from a storage item at a glance. info Rune Point sharing matches the priest's and Allied Spirit's cults by their Rqid - something cults never needed before this release, so an older cult item in your world may not have one. The Rune Magic casting dialog now tells you explicitly when a bonded Allied Spirit exists but isn't recognized as sharing a cult, instead of the source picker just silently not appearing, and the Add Rqids dialog that pops up during migrations now includes cults that lack Rqids, so it can fix this for you. #1004

#999 A spirit trapped in an item via a Binding Enchantment can now be linked from that item's sheet by dragging the spirit's actor onto it. It is possible to bind multiple spirits into one item, letting a single Foundry item represent something like a handful of bound crystals. Once bound, whoever holds the item - in other words, has it equipped - can cast any Spirit Magic spell the spirit itself knows, shown under its own "Bound Spirit:" divider. Casting can also draw on the bound spirit's own Magic Points, which get their own entry in the Magic Point Source Order popout. Draining a bound spirit's Magic Points to zero releases it from the binding, and a cast that would do that prompts for confirmation first. The cap of CHA / 3 total bound spirits is shown as an informational count on the Combat tab, with a warning if you go over it - since too many bound spirits should provoke a spirit rebellion.

#959 #1021 Any Gear, Weapon, or Armor item can now carry a Spell Matrix Enchantment: drag a Spirit Magic spell onto the item's sheet to enchant it, and from then on whoever has that item equipped can cast that spell, whether or not they personally know it. Casting it works straight from the actor sheet on its own entry on the Spirit Magic tab under a "Matrix:" divider, alongside any existing "Allied Spirit:" and "Bound Spirit:" dividers. It uses the caster's own POW×5 chance and their own Magic Points, drawn through the same source picker as any other spell. A matrix spell doesn't count against the holder's own CHA spell-point limit, since it was never one of their personally-learned spells. An item isn't limited to one enchanted spell either: drop additional Spirit Magic spells onto the same item and each gets its own chip on the item sheet, with its own GM-only points field and its own delete button (points are only editable when the underlying spell is variable - a fixed-level spell shows its points read-only). In practice that means you could, for example, have several matrix-enchanted spells embedded in a single sword. The old "Held in Matrix" checkbox on a personal spell is now deprecated Before this release, the closest thing to a matrix was the "Held in Matrix" checkbox on a character's own Spirit Magic spell (isMatrix) - it only ever excluded that spell from the caster's own CHA spell-point limit, with no connection to a gear item. GMs ended up overloading that one checkbox for two different situations: a real physical matrix, or a bound/allied spirit's spell copied onto the character just so it wouldn't count against their CHA limit. This release's Allied Spirit and Bound Spirit spell-sharing now handles the second case properly, so the checkbox is superseded - it still exists and still works exactly as before, but should be treated as deprecated. There's no fully automatic migration for it, and there can't reasonably be one: nothing in the data says which of the two situations above an isMatrix spell represents, and for the real-matrix case, nothing says which physical item (if any) it was meant to live in - both are always a GM call. To make it easier to find and convert them, a "Migrate isMatrix Spells" macro in the "System Macros" compendium (folder "RuneQuest Glorantha System/Macros") lists every isMatrix spell in the world, with the actor and spell as clickable links and the spell's Focus text shown - many GMs use that field to note which item a matrix should live in. Each row lets you handle that spell at your own pace: Create Gear - creates a new Gear item on the same actor with the Spell Matrix Enchantment already linked at the same points, and opens it for you to rename. Delete Spirit Magic (with a confirmation prompt) - removes the now-obsolete original Spirit Magic item, once you're happy with its replacement or once you've set up the bonded spirit's proper spell-sharing instead. Neither action fires until you choose it, and a row you resolve just stops showing up the next time the macro runs. Not an embedded copy of the spell Enchanting a matrix only stores a link to the spell (a Rqid) plus the number of points enchanted into it - the spell's own mechanics are never embedded on the item or copied onto it. Every time the matrix is cast, the system resolves that Rqid fresh against whatever world or compendium item currently matches it, so a later correction to the spell (or an update to the compendium it came from) is picked up automatically instead of the matrix carrying a stale copy. It's a new way for an item to grant a spell in this system - the same Rqid lookup that already backs cross-references elsewhere, applied here to resolve a spell's mechanics live rather than storing them.

#512 #1028 #1035 Magic Points now recover on their own as game time passes, computed straight from Foundry's world clock. Advancing that clock is a calendar module's job (e.g. Calendaria, GG Calendar, or Seasons & Stars) - Foundry itself has no built-in way to move it forward, so without one there's no game time for this to catch up against. Simply opening a character's sheet is enough to catch it up, and so is the world clock advancing while the sheet is already open. A new recovery-rate indicator next to Magic Points on the character header shows the resulting points/day and time-per-point on hover. A gift or HeroQuest effect that speeds up or slows down recovery can target the new system.attributes.magicPointRecoveryRateFactor field directly with an Active Effect - e.g., a Humakti gift doubling recovery speed could OVERRIDE this to 2, in effect halving the time it takes to recover a Magic Point. For GMs who'd rather not have any silent auto-recovery at all, a new Automatic Magic Point Recovery world setting turns this off entirely, so Magic Point recovery goes back to being applied by hand. The default for this setting is on, so you need to opt out if you don't want this.

#436 #1031 #1035 Natural Hit Point healing now works the same way as Magic Point recovery: it's computed from elapsed game time instead of anything applied by hand. Each wounded hit location recovers its own healing rate in points, applied as a lump at the end of each elapsed game week rather than prorated, matching the Core rule. A location with more than one wound splits the recovered points evenly across them, with any remainder going to the lightest wound, and a severed or useless location's hit points still recover naturally even though regaining the use of the limb still takes magic capable of regrowing it. This only applies to player-owned characters - NPCs are unaffected and still need their healing applied by hand, same as before. Whether a character was actually resting - which Core requires for natural healing to apply - isn't tracked or enforced either: healing is applied automatically each elapsed game week regardless. There's no per-character override for this; the only control is the Automatic Natural Healing world setting, which turns automatic healing off entirely for GMs who'd rather enforce that condition by hand instead. The default is on, so you need to opt out if you don't want this.

#912 A new menu item on the actor sheet header opens a single-screen session listing every pending Experience check on the character at once - skills, Runes, Passions, and POW - with an optional Roll All action and a fixed/random gain toggle, instead of working through each one's own Improve dialog in turn. Each row in the session shows what you need to know to make the call before rolling: The Fixed | Random selector (top left) chooses whether a successful improvement gains a fixed amount or a random one - what that amount actually is differs by improvement type, and is shown on each row (see the +1d3-1 vs +1d6% in the screenshot below). The pill next to each item shows the target you need to roll to improve: under a value for Runes, over a value for everything else. Hovering it shows a tooltip explaining how that value was calculated. Rolling through the per-item improvements leaves a summary of how each improvement attempt went, so at the end you will have an overview of how lucky you were. Rolling also generates chat messages for the improvement rolls, and if you do a "Roll All" you get a combined chat message for all the rolls at once.

#1033 The hit-location visualization on the Combat tab - previously laid out for humanoid actors only - now recognizes quadruped creatures too, based on their hit locations, and shows them against their own silhouette (head, forequarters, hindquarters, legs) instead of a default table layout.

Fix Active Effect duration units reading the wrong (deprecated) property and localizing to a key that doesn't exist in Foundry v14, which logged a warning on every render #992 #993 Stop shipping a duplicate manifest in the release package, which broke the Forge's package caching #1000 Allow a natural or hit-location-linked weapon (fist, bite, claw, etc.) to leave its own Hit Points unset instead of forcing them to 0, since it uses the owning hit location's HP instead #1012 Fix the Spirit Magic tab's points input rendering far wider than intended in edit mode, throwing off row alignment #1016 Fix the actor sheet's drag-and-drop highlight getting stuck on, instead of clearing, when a drag moves onto an overlapping Item Sheet #1025
This is a pure bugfix release with just one fix.
World migration fails for actors with owned items that have Active Effects. #1043

This release's headline feature is spell effects. Cast a spell such as Bladesharp, Protection or Strength, and when it takes effect, the target's owner clicks Apply on the chat card to put the spell's effect on the right actor or weapon, with the right level and duration. Casting the same spell again, or a spell that can't share a target with one already there, is handled for you, and every spell on a token shows at the top of the token HUD, where the GM can open, remove or add one. It builds on resisted spells: a spell like Sleep or Befuddle now hands the target's owner a card to resist or accept, and rolls POW against POW on the resistance table. Active Effects get more capable too: an effect on an actor can now change the actor's items, such as one skill, every hit location, or the weapon it's on. Alongside that, a new actor can start from a template actor, and many more things can be dragged to the hotbar.

#1078 The spell card now shows one row per target, saying whether the spell took effect. If the outcome needs a judgment call, the GM can rule on each row: takes effect, or no effect. When the spell took effect, the target's owner gets an Apply button. Clicking it puts the spell's effect on the target: A spell that works on a weapon, like Bladesharp or Fireblade, goes on the target's equipped weapon it fits, and asks which one if there's more than one. Any other spell goes on the target itself. The effect is named after the spell and its level, like "Bladesharp (3)", and lasts the spell's duration: 2 minutes for spirit magic, 15 minutes for rune magic. A few effects have a longer duration of their own, like Catseye's 12 hours.

The spell effects ship with wiki module 2.1.0, which has an effect for every spirit and rune spell that lasts for a while. Some change the sheet, like Strength raising STR or Bladesharp adding to the weapon's attack and damage. The others are reminders that show the spell is active until it runs out. See the Wiki 2.1.0 release notes for the full list. Update the wiki module first Update the RQG wiki module to 2.1.0 before the system. When the world is upgraded, the migration links the spells already on your actors to their effects by looking them up in the wiki module's compendiums. If the wiki module is still the old version, those spells get no effect link. If that happens, update the wiki module and run the migration again: as the GM, click Trigger World Migration in the Game Settings sidebar tab. The world reloads and migrates again, and this time the spells get their links. Links that are already there are left alone, so running it again is safe.

Casting a spell on a target that already has the same spell active has no effect (Core p.255 Q&A), and some spells can't be on the same target at once. For example, Bladesharp and Fireblade can't share a weapon, and neither can Protection and Shimmer on a person. When a spell has no effect for one of these reasons, Apply tells you why and the card records it. Only the target's owner sees the reason. The world setting Recast Spells Take Effect chooses how a recast of the same spell is handled: Never, the Q&A read literally; Only if stronger (the default), where a higher level replaces a weaker casting; or Always, a house rule where every new casting replaces the old one and refreshes its duration. #1332

#1170 Berserker and Fanaticism now change the rolls of whoever has them, and the roll dialogs show it: Berserker: attacks get half again, or double against a creature with the Chaos rune. Parrying, dodging and casting aren't allowed: the dialog says why and can't roll. CON is increased by half, CON rolls succeed at 95%, and the berserker has Countermagic 2, or 4 against spells from chaotic casters. When the spell ends, the berserker becomes Helpless. Berserker replaces a Fanaticism on the target. Fanaticism: attacks get half again, parrying isn't allowed and Dodge is halved. Which spells a fanatic may still cast is up to the GM. Being preserved from shock and unconsciousness while berserk is also up to the GM. The harpy in the wiki module now has the Chaos rune.

A token's spell effects are shown at the top of the token HUD's status palette, above the condition markers, with their name, the item they're on and the time left. The GM can click one to open it, right-click to remove it, or change its level on the effect's sheet. Hovering over an effect also says what it does. Has automated effects means it changes the sheet or its spell's rules act while it is on, like Bladesharp or Warding. Only marks the spell while it lasts means the GM rules on what it does, like Befuddle. A partly automated effect adds what is left to the GM, for example "Not automated: −1 strike rank" on Mobility. When a spell runs out, its effect is removed from the token and its item. The GM can also add a spell effect without casting, for example for a spell cast before the scene started. Click the + in the same section, search for the spell, set its level, and click Add.

Because spells now show on tokens as spell effects, the token HUD's status palette no longer holds spell markers. Protection, Strength, Bladesharp and the other spell statuses are gone, and so are Ironhand, Parry and the 1–6 counters. The counters were a way to note a spell's level, which the spell effect's name now shows. The palette now has general condition markers only. The new ones are Helpless, Concentrating, In Spirit Combat, Discorporate, Possessed, Invisible, Flying and Burning, and Restrained is now called Immobilized. Upgrading A spell status that is already on a token when you upgrade stays on it as an ordinary effect until it runs out. You can also delete it from the actor's Effects tab. For a spell that has no spell effect yet, add a plain effect on the actor's Effects tab.

#1171 The heal button on a hit location now opens one dialog for the whole actor. It lists every wounded location with its hit points and wounds, with the clicked location's largest wound selected. Heal one wound by up to the chosen points, the way First Aid treats one injury at a time, or switch to Remove All Damage to clear every location at once. A severed limb is no longer reattached just because 6 or more points were healed on it. Tick Reattach next to its wounds instead, since whether all parts are at hand is the GM's call. Heal, Heal Wound and Heal Body now heal when you click Apply on their cast card: Heal puts its points on one location. Click a wound to heal it first; the rest of the points go to the location's other wounds. With 6 points it can reattach a severed limb. Heal Wound heals as many hit points as the magic points spent with it. Click the dots under each wound to choose where the healing goes. With 6 magic points it can reattach one severed limb. Heal Body heals every location and the total hit points, and reattaches severed limbs. First Aid works the same way. Target the wounded token, or no one to treat yourself, and roll First Aid. On a success the roll card gets an Apply button: it asks which wound to treat, then rolls the healing (1D3, 2D3 on a special, 1D3+3 on a critical) for that wound. On a fumble Apply asks which location was treated and does 1D3 damage to it instead. Stopping bleeding and treating each injury only once are still up to the GM. This needs the wiki module.

#920 Active Effects that change a value on the actor's items have a new, more versatile key format. Before, such a change had to use the Custom change type and could only add to the value. Now it can use all of Foundry's change types. For example, it can raise one skill, add armor to every hit location, or improve the weapon it's on. Start the change's key with @, followed by which items to change, a :, and the path of the value: Key Changes Example @<rqid>:system.<path> The actor's item with that rqid @i.skill.dodge:system.baseChance, add 10 @~<regex>:system.<path> Every item whose rqid matches the regular expression @~^i\.hit-location\.:system.naturalAp, add 2 @.:system.<path> The item the effect is on @.:system.effect.add.melee.attack on a weapon, add 10 Change types: these changes use Foundry's normal types, Add, Multiply, Override, Upgrade and Downgrade, just like any other key. Keys that don't start with @ work exactly as they do in Foundry. Weapon bonuses: the system.effect.add values are bonuses added on top of a value. A weapon has them for melee and missile attack, parry and damage. The damage bonus is new in this release, and a weapon's rolled damage never goes below 0. Spell level: in an effect that comes from a spell, @level in the value is the level the spell was cast at. For example, Bladesharp adds @level * 5 to attack. Warnings: a key that can't be used, such as a mistyped rqid, an rqid the actor has no item for, or a change type a bonus can't use, shows the GM a warning saying what's wrong. When the world loads, these are collected into one summary. See Rqid for the bonus values you can change and more examples. Changed keys Before this release, a key like i.skill.dodge:system.baseChance on the Custom change type changed an item. The world migration rewrites these to the new form, @i.skill.dodge:system.baseChance on Add, so they keep doing the same thing. A key in the old form that the migration can't reach, such as one typed afterwards or in a module's compendium, shows the GM a warning and does nothing until it's updated.

documents.t: #1168 Spells that affect a place, like Shake Earth, Warding or Sanctify, now make a scene Region. The caster places it, snapped to the scene's grid, and the squares or hexes it will cover light up as it moves: Ranged spells must lie wholly within range, centered on a point the caster can see. The scene is dimmed outside what the caster's token can see within range, and the area can't be placed there. For a point the caster perceives by magic, the GM places it in sight and then drags the Region where it belongs. Rituals can be placed anywhere, as a ritual is held where its area is. A ward is placed by clicking its four wands. The GM and the caster's players see the area; a spell like Mist Cloud is seen by everyone. The area ends when the spell does, and the GM can move or delete it like any Region. With the wiki module, Shake Earth hinders everyone inside, wards strike hostile intruders and stop spells cast from outside, and Sanctify tells the caster when a non-initiate or a spell crosses into it. info Spell areas measure true distance in meters, as the rules do. On square grids, Foundry's default counts a diagonal step as one space, so the movement ruler lets tokens go about 40% farther diagonally than the rules allow. Set Configure Settings → Core → Grid Diagonals to Exact to make the ruler and the spell areas agree. Hex and gridless scenes aren't affected. See Setting Up Scenes.

#757 #758 #1066 #1076 #1077 A spell that the target can resist, like Sleep, Befuddle or Slow, now checks its target before any magic points are spent. The cast dialog picks the target from the tokens you can see, nearest first, or yourself. Cast with no target, the card waits for the GM to rule on it; a spell that can only go on you or your weapon, like Bladesharp, goes on you. The cast then posts a single card to the target's owner, who chooses Resist or Accept. The resistance roll pits the caster's POW against the target's POW on the resistance table. The target doesn't see which spell it is until it takes effect. Before anyone resists, each target's Countermagic, Shield or ward meets the spell, and a spell they stop has no effect on that target and asks for no roll. This works for every spell, automated or not. A cast is settled on the GM's client, so a GM must be logged in for a spell to get past its cast roll. A spell cast while no GM is connected waits on its card and goes on when one logs in. Some spells resist differently: One roll per target. Turn Undead and Teleportation can be cast at several targets, and each target resists or accepts on its own card. Turn Undead reaches one undead per point. No POW. A side without POW resists with its current magic points instead, caster and target alike (RBM p.6), so undead resist Turn Undead with their magic points. An empty POW and a POW of 0 both count as none. A target with neither can't resist: its card says so and the spell takes effect. #1332 Spirit combat. Bind Ghost and Resurrect only work if the caster wins spirit combat. Until spirit combat is automated, the cast card waits for the GM to rule whether the caster won. Area spells. Harmony and Inviolable make one resistance roll for everyone within their radius, the caster included, and the card says what it overcomes, for example "affects POW 15 or lower". Inviolable's own text reads the resistance table the other way round; it uses the same reading as Harmony and every other resistance roll. The cast dialog lights up the area and targets everyone in it for you. Reflection. A spell that fails against a target protected by Reflection is sent back at its caster. The caster's own Countermagic or Shield meets it first, then the caster resists it with their own POW. A spell is only reflected once. #1178 The GM can also send any resistance roll to a player, for example STR against a trap, from the actor sheet's Combat tab, the combat tracker, the Actors sidebar, or a Token HUD button. The Token HUD button can be turned off in the settings.

#636 #778 #1055 Foundry's Create Actor dialog has a new Start from choice. Blank works as before, and Choose template... opens a list of template actors from the world and the compendiums. The wiki module provides templates for adventurers, like "Human (Base)" and "Mostali (Dwarf)", and for creatures, like animals, chaos monsters, elementals, mounts and spirits. Search the list by name, or filter it by class, role and species. The new actor is a copy of the template, with all its items. See Creating an Adventurer for how to make your own actors show up as templates.

documents.t: #402 #874 #1059 #1060 A weapon on the hotbar now opens its attack dialog, and a spirit or rune magic spell opens its cast dialog. Items on the actor sheet's Combat tab, including Dodge, can be dragged to the hotbar. A compendium on the hotbar opens it, a journal page opens its journal at that page, and a scene views it. Ammunition that can't attack on its own, like arrows, and folders show a warning instead of making a macro that doesn't work.

#1166 A few item fields used to store the text shown in the language the item was edited in: a passion, a rune's type, an armor's type and material, and a weapon's combat maneuvers. An item from a module in another language then showed in that language, a passion lost its image, and a combat maneuver only got its default damage type when its name matched the language of the world. These fields now store a value from the list as a key, and show it in the language of the world. Text that isn't in the list is kept as typed. On the sheet you can type or pick a value in the language of the world or in English. Item names, like "Loyalty (Clan)" or "Cuirass (Leather)", don't change. They stay in the language they were written in, until the item is saved on its sheet again. The sheet then builds the name in the language of the world, with that language's word order, and leaves out empty parts: armor without a prefix or material, or a skill without a specialization, no longer gets a stray space or empty parentheses. Links to other items and journal entries, like a spell's description or a weapon's skill, now show the name of what they link to, in the language of the world. They used to show the name it had when the link was made, in the language of whoever made it. Lists of links are sorted by name. #1167 Upgrading The world migration saves the keys for the items in the world and on its actors. Items in compendiums, including other modules' compendiums, are converted each time they're loaded, so they need nothing.

#769 #1306 Links on sheets, like a spell's description, a spell's effect, a weapon's skill or a cult's runes, now show when they're broken. A link to something the world can't find, for example because its module isn't active or it was deleted, gets a warning sign and a red dashed border, with the last part of its rqid as its name. Hover it to see the full rqid. Before, a broken link looked like any other link, so you only found out when you clicked it. When something with that rqid is added to the world, open sheets show the link's name again right away. Every link also shows the current name of what it links to, so two links to the same skill look the same. Before, they could keep different names and look like links to two different skills. See Rqid for how links find what they point to.

#1129 #1131 The system now has a documented API, game.system.api, for macros and modules. A macro can roll skills, runes, passions and characteristics, attack with a weapon, and cast spirit and rune magic, with the roll dialog or without it. It can also read a character's skills, weapon attacks and the spells they can cast, including spells from an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a spell matrix. Values stored on a character, like hit points and magic points, are read straight from the character data, which is now also part of the API. See the API overview to get started, and the macro examples for ready-to-use macros. From now on, changes that can break macros or modules are listed in the release notes.

actor.applyDamage(...) is gone. Use actor.damage({ amount, location, armorPoints }) to damage a hit location, where location is a hit location item or "random" and armorPoints (default the location's own armor) is subtracted first, and actor.heal({ location, points, wound, restoreSevered }) to heal one. Both return what they did. item.applyWound(...) and item.healWound(...) on hit location items are gone too; use actor.damage and actor.heal. #1171 A rune's system.runeType is now the type itself, like "power", instead of { type, name }. Read item.system.runeType where you read item.system.runeType.type. system.passion on a passion, system.armorType and system.material on armor, and the name of a weapon's combat maneuvers hold a key for a value from the list, like "Loyalty", "HeavyLeather" or "HeadButt", and the typed text for any other value. The attack hooks' combatManeuver.name is that same value. To show a key, localize it with its prefix: RQG.Item.Passion.PassionEnum., RQG.Item.Armor.ArmorType., RQG.Item.Armor.ArmorMaterial. or RQG.Item.Weapon.combatManeuver.. #1166 Rqid links no longer have a name. To show one, use game.system.api.rqid.nameFromRqid(link.rqid). #1167

Rolls now have one method each, taking an options object: item.roll(options) rolls a skill, rune or passion. actor.rollCharacteristic(name, options) rolls a characteristic. actor.rollReputation(options) rolls Reputation. item.cast(options) casts a spirit or rune magic spell as its owner, and actor.castSpell(spell, options) casts one with that actor as the caster, including spells from an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a matrix. item.attack({ usage }) opens the attack dialog for a weapon, with usage preselected. Without skipDialog: true they open the roll dialog. With it they roll at once and return the roll. actor.addSpellEffect({ token }) opens the token HUD's Add a Spell Effect dialog for the actor, so modules can offer it too. Modules can change and react to rolls with hooks: Prepare the roll Before the roll After the roll rqg.prepareAbilityRoll rqg.preAbilityRoll rqg.abilityRoll rqg.prepareCharacteristicRoll rqg.preCharacteristicRoll rqg.characteristicRoll rqg.prepareReputationRoll rqg.preReputationRoll rqg.reputationRoll rqg.prepareSpellCast rqg.preSpellCast rqg.spellCast rqg.prepareAttack rqg.preAttack rqg.attack rqg.prepareDefence rqg.preDefence rqg.defence A "prepare" hook adds modifiers to the roll, or says why the roll isn't allowed, for example a berserker's parry. The roll dialog shows both before Roll is clicked, so the chance in the dialog is the chance that's rolled. A "pre" hook runs once, when the roll is made, and can cancel it. See Roll hooks. Modules can also make a skill do something after it's rolled, the way the wiki module's First Aid heals a wound, and a spell's effect can change rolls through roll entries, like Berserker and Fanaticism. A spell's behavior can also make a spell area on the scene, limit how many targets the spell reaches, roll its damage and hit location like an attack, and give the caster's players control of its target while it lasts, as Command (cult spirit) does. See Behaviors. The old methods still work until RQG 6.4.0, but log a warning in the browser console that names the replacement: Old method Replacement item.abilityRoll / item.abilityRollImmediate item.roll actor.characteristicRoll / actor.characteristicRollImmediate actor.rollCharacteristic actor.reputationRoll / actor.reputationRollImmediate actor.rollReputation item.spiritMagicRoll / item.spiritMagicRollImmediate item.cast item.runeMagicRoll / item.runeMagicRollImmediate item.cast Hotbar macros made by dragging a skill to the hotbar in earlier versions use the old method. To update one, drag the skill to the hotbar again. #1132

documents.t: rolls.spiritMagic and rolls.runeMagic take a magicPointSource, to draw the magic points from the character, an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a magic point storage item instead of following the character's draw order. actor.getMagicPointSources() lists the sources, with their magic points. See Character data. The spirit and rune magic dialogs start with the options given, like levelUsed, magicPointBoost, magicPointSource and rollMode, and the player can still change them. See Rolls. dialogs.addWound and dialogs.healWounds open the character sheet's Add Wound and Heal Wounds dialogs for a hit location. addWound can start with a damage and with the armor and total hit points boxes set. See Character data. #1136

The newer character and item sheets are the default. Their names end in V2, like "Character Sheet V2". The old sheets, like "Character Sheet" and "Passion Item Sheet", can still be picked in a document's Sheet configuration, but they will be removed in RQG 6.3.0. Actors and items set to an old sheet then open in the V2 sheet automatically, so there's nothing you need to do. Until then, opening an old sheet logs a warning in the browser console.

documents.t: Spells link to their effect with an Effect field on the spell sheet, next to the description link. Spells already on actors get their link from the compendium during the world migration. #1086 Spells have a Resisted By field that says how a target can resist them: a resistance roll against one target or each target, spirit combat, or nothing. A creature without POW resists with its magic points, so leave its POW empty rather than 0. #1068 Spells record what they can be cast on and what kind of effect they have, in two new fields. #1080 Passions, rune types, armor types and materials, and combat maneuver names can be stored as keys, like passion: Loyalty or armorType: Cuirass, so the same content shows in the language of each world. Text in English or in the language of the world still works and is turned into the key when it's loaded. Translation modules need no change, since they already translate these keys. #1166 Translation modules can also change how the sheets put item names together. Each item type that builds its name has a pattern key, like RQG.Item.Armor.NamePattern, {armorType} ({material}) in English, which a language can reorder, for example {armorType} de {material}. Armor adds its prefix with a second key, RQG.Item.Armor.NamePrefixPattern, {prefix} {name} in English. #1166 Rqid links only need the rqid. A name on a link is ignored and isn't saved, since the link shows the name of what it finds. #1167 Errors and warnings now carry a code like RQG-W-0012, which makes them easier to report and look up.

This is the first release built on the modernized compendium data pipeline. It's a fresh-start release rather than a content update — no intentional gameplay or content changes were made. Its sole purpose is to establish a clean baseline that's fully aligned with the current fvtt-system-rqg data models. Compendium data is now validated against JSON Schemas generated live from the fvtt-system-rqg DataModels. This caught a batch of pre-existing content bugs — misspelled or renamed fields, invalid null values on non-nullable fields, and similar issues — that had gone unnoticed until now. This release requires rqg system v6.0.0+ and Foundry v14+. If you're running an older system version, stay on the previous release (v1.3.5) for now.

Every Spirit Magic spell had broken Rqid flags (its language tag was a translation placeholder that never actually resolved), so nothing could look a spell up directly by its rqid - most notably rqg system 6.1.0's new Spell Matrix Enchantment item feature, which failed to find any Spirit Magic spell dragged onto it from this compendium. Spells your characters had already learned were never affected by this - only fresh lookups by rqid were broken, so this only becomes relevant once you're running rqg system 6.1.0+. Unbalanced HTML tags in several bestiary, rune magic, skill, and homeland description entries could make parts of the text render incorrectly - all now fixed. The Discorporation spell's "see also" link and Create Fissure's reference to the falling rules were both dead placeholder links that never got filled in - Discorporation now links to the correct spell, and Create Fissure now cites the core rulebook (RQG p156) directly.

The build pipeline now automatically checks @RQID[...] cross-references, HTML structure, other Foundry document links, and local asset file references against the actual compendium content on every push, to catch this class of bug going forward before it ships.

RQG does not require any modules (except for the RQG wiki module), but it is a goal that it should work with as many as possible. Here is a list of modules and their current state in regards to this RQG system. A checked checkbox means that it should work in the latest released version of RQG.

Calendar modules (e.g. Calendaria, GG Calendar, or Seasons & Stars) that advance Foundry's world clock - since v6.1.0, Magic Points recover automatically as that clock moves forward. A proper Gloranthan calendar (Theyalan seasons, weeks, and holy days) is not implemented yet, see issue #900. Dice So Nice The system is DsN aware and handles when rolls are made for things like the attack chats.

Token Action HUD should be added as a separate integration module. Item Piles This need a little more investigation to make it understand what items are unique. An incomplete setting can be found at Item-Pile-settings.

The RQG system has an API that macros and modules can use to roll dice, cast spells and read information about characters. It's available in Foundry as game.system.api. If you write macros to automate things at your table, or build a module that works with RQG, the API has two parts: The character data, actor.system and item.system. Read values that are stored on a character, like characteristics, hit points or a cult's Rune Points, straight from there, and change them with Foundry's actor.update and item.update. The fields are described in Character data. game.system.api, for everything that needs the rules, like rolling dice and casting spells. Modules can also call the roll methods on RQG's actors and items, and actor.damage, actor.heal, actor.getCastableSpells and actor.getMagicPointSources. Don't call other methods on them or use other parts of the system directly. Those can change in any release.

Rolls – roll skills, runes, passions and characteristics, attack with weapons and cast spirit and rune magic. Roll hooks – react to rolls, add modifiers, or forbid a parry or dodge. Character data – read skills, castable spells, hit points, magic points, rune points and other values from a character. Item data – the fields of every item type, and which are calculated or effect targets. Behaviors – make a spell or skill do something when Apply is clicked, like Dispel Magic removing spells or First Aid healing a wound. Macro examples – ready-to-use macros to start from. RQG System ID (rqid) – find the best version of a document by its RQG id. Maintenance – run the world migration by hand, with a dry run, and fix invalid data and missing rqids.

Wherever the API needs an actor you can give it an actor, a token, or the name, id or uuid of one. If you leave the actor out, the first selected token is used, or else your assigned character. Wherever it needs an item you can give it the item itself, or its rqid, name, id or uuid. Prefer the rqid ("i.skill.scan"): it works in worlds using any language and after the item is renamed. A name ("Scan") works too, for example for homebrew items without an rqid. If something can't be found, the API shows an error notification and stops the macro.

The API follows the RQG system version. When a system update changes the API or moves or renames a field in the character data in a way that can break macros or modules, the release notes say so. Check them when updating the system.

When the system replaces a method, a field or a syntax, the old one keeps working for a while. Using it logs a deprecation warning in the browser console (press F12), once per session. The warning names what to use instead, the version that deprecated it and the version that removes it, for example deprecated since Version RQG 6.2.0 / removed in Version RQG 6.4.0. The old way stays for at least one minor version, usually two, before it is removed. The removal version is fixed when the deprecation is announced, and the release notes list it. Update your macros and modules while the warning is showing. After the removal version the old call stops working.

A behavior is a small script in a module that makes a spell or a skill do something when Apply is clicked on its chat card: Dispel Magic removes spells, Summon Earth Elemental places a token, First Aid heals a wound. A spell's behavior can also change rolls while its effect is active, like Berserker forbidding a parry. The wiki module's spells and skills are built this way, and a module of your own can add behaviors for other spells and skills, or replace the wiki's. A spell that only needs to add a bonus or show that it's active doesn't need a behavior. An effect template does that without code.

A module registers its behaviors from a hook, keyed by the rqid of the spell or skill: // scripts/my-behaviors.mjs, listed under esmodules in your module.json const source = { lang: "en", priority: 10 }; Hooks.once("rqg.registerSpellBehaviors", (registry) => { registry.register("i.rune-magic.summon-wind-child", spellBehavior, source); }); Hooks.once("rqg.registerSkillBehaviors", (registry) => { registry.register("i.skill.treat-poison", skillBehavior, source); }); What is the same for spells and skills: Registration. Both hooks are called once, at Foundry's setup, after every module's init, so game.system.api is available when you register. Register from there: a later register call on a registry you kept also counts, but only from then on. Matching. Behaviors are found by rqid, not by name. They work in a world in another language, and for your own copy of a spell or skill with the same rqid. Which module wins. If more than one module registers a behavior for the same rqid, the one in the world's language wins, then the highest priority. A module of your own with a higher priority than the wiki module replaces the wiki's behavior. A behavior is replaced whole. The winning registration is used as it is, never merged with the others for that rqid. To change one part of the wiki's behavior, register a complete behavior with every part you want to keep. Who gets Apply. The card shows Apply for each target, but only to the target's owners and the GM. apply runs on the client of the user who clicks it. What apply returns. { outcome: "resolved" } when it has done its work, which uses up the Apply. Return nothing to leave Apply clickable, for example when the user cancelled a dialog. Errors. A behavior that throws is caught and reported, so one broken spell or skill doesn't stop the others.

Hooks.once("rqg.registerSpellBehaviors", (registry) => { registry.register( "i.rune-magic.summon-wind-child", { // Players can't create tokens, so run on the GM's client runAsGm: true, apply: (scope) targetName, the target Apply was clicked for targetToken, the token it is cast at, when that is known, else undefined cast, with the spellRqid of the spell cast ("" when it has none), the level cast at, the magicPointsSpent and runePointsSpent, the casterSuccessLevel, and the caster: their actorUuid and the tokenUuid they cast from ("" when they cast without a token) duration, what the effect of It runs on the active GM's client, once per target, right after a successful cast roll and before anyone resists, or, when the spell is added from the token HUD, on the client of whoever adds it. Return { outcome: "stopped" } to stop the incoming spell, or { outcome: "pass" } to let it through. It doesn't run for a spell the target casts on itself. It runs after the barriers, so use it for defenses that aren't a strength, like a custom check. Spells that register the same onIncomingSpell function are decided together. onResisted gets the same as onIncomingSpell. It runs when the actor's resistance roll held against a spell, by roll or by GM ruling, on the active GM's client. Show the target's owners anything they should see with a whispered chat message, since a notification would only reach the GM. Return { outcome: "reflected" } to send the spell back at its caster. The caster's own onIncomingSpell spells meet it first, and if they let it through, the system posts a new resistance card aimed at the caster: their POW when they cast it against their POW now. A reflected spell is never reflected again. Every hook but apply runs on the active GM's client, which is where a cast's state changes, so a GM must be logged in for a cast to get past its cast roll. apply runs on the client of whoever clicks Apply, so the target's owner can be asked which weapon or which wounds. onEnd gets { effect }, the effect that ended. An effect that expired is deleted after its onEnd has run. A spell whose effect is a place uses game.system.api.spellEffects.createArea(scope, options) in its apply. The caster places the area on the canvas, snapped to the scene's grid with the squares or hexes it covers highlighted: within the spell's range for a Ranged spell, anywhere for the rest, as a ritual is held where its area is. A Ranged spell's area must also be centered on a point the caster's token can see: the scene is dimmed outside that, and placement there is refused. options.shape is { kind: "circle", radius } or { kind: "square", side } in meters, the square rotated with the mouse wheel, or { kind: "polygon", corners, maxArea }, clicked corner by corner, like a ward's wands, and no larger than maxArea square meters. placement: "caster" puts a circle or square around the caster's token instead. duration overrides the spell's own, and visible: true shows the area to every player; otherwise only the GM and the caster's players see it. An area with a duration puts an effect on the caster, so it ends when the spell does; with duration: null the Region is the spell and lasts until it is deleted. The GM can move or delete the Region either way. onAreaEnter and onAreaExit get { spell, cast, region, token, actor, crossed }; crossed is false for a token that was inside when the area appeared. In onAreaEnter, spellEffects.applyAreaEffect(scope) puts the spell's effect template on the token; the system takes it off when the token leaves or the area goes. onSpellAcross gets { spell, cast, region, incomingSpell, incomingCast, targets }: this area's spell, the spell cast across its boundary, and the tokens inside it that were targeted. It runs once per area and cast, before the targets' protective spells meet the incoming spell. The wiki's wards sound their alarm this way. Any Region behavior can have one.

A protective spell says what it gives, and the system judges. barrier is { priority: number; // lower is met first, further out, like Active Effect change priority strength(effect, cast): number; // a spell of at most this many points is stopped usedUp: "never" | "unlessLayerTwoStronger"; onUsedUp?(effect): Promise<void>; // instead of deleting the effect } cast is the incoming cast: its castPoints, and its caster, so a barrier can depend on who casts. A strength of 0 or less gives no layer, and so does one that throws or isn't a number. A barrier whose priority isn't a number is skipped, and one with an unknown usedUp is never used up; both log a warning in the browser console. The system walks the layers of the target's effects, and of the Regions it is in (below), from the lowest priority up: Layers are met in a row, at full strength. A spell that gets through one meets the next one undiminished. Equal priority is one layer. Only the strongest effect there counts, and its usedUp applies. This is how Countermagic doesn't stack. A module that wants a barrier of its own picks its own priority. usedUp: "unlessLayerTwoStronger" is Countermagic's rule: a spell 2 or more points weaker is stopped and the effect stays, a spell within 1 point of it is stopped and the effect is used up, and a spell 2 or more points stronger breaks it and goes on. The system deletes the effect, or calls onUsedUp when there is one. A target's own defenses don't stop a spell it casts itself, and spells with Gets through Countermagic and Shield pass every barrier. The system's own layers are in game.system.api.spellEffects.barrierPriorities, with gaps so a module can go between them: { area: 100, consumable: 200, lasting: 300 } area is for spell areas and other Regions, consumable for layers a spell uses up, like Countermagic, and lasting for layers that stay, like Shield. Priorities aren't checked: a module could put an inner defense outside a ward. Document it, and the GM can see it. Protection, which only counts for armor, isn't a barrier. // A made-up defense that counts as Countermagic, but only against spirits registry.register( "i.spirit-magic.spirit-screen", { barrier: { priority: game.system.api.spellEffects.barrierPriorities.consumable, strength: (effect, cast) => (isSpirit(cast.caster) ? effect.system.spell.level : 0), usedUp: "unlessLayerTwoStronger", }, }, source, ); areaBarrier is the same for a spell's area (createArea): the tokens inside it get the layer against spells cast from outside the area. Its strength(areaCast, incomingCast, target) gets the area's own cast, the incoming one and the token it protects, so a ward can leave out its caster's enemies. The wiki's wards declare it.

Any Foundry Region behavior can take part, not only a spell's area, so a module can make a place that isn't a cast spell, like a standing temple ward or a Chaos-tainted area. Write an ordinary RegionBehaviorType and add the methods the system looks for: class ChaosTaint extends foundry.data.regionBehaviors.RegionBehaviorType { static defineSchema() { return { strength: new foundry.data.fields.NumberField({ initial: 3 }) }; } // A spell cast from outside the Region at tokens inside it async onSpellAcross({ region, behavior, incomingSpell, incomingCast, targets }) {} // A layer that spells cast from outside the Region must get through get barrier() { return { priority: game.system.api.spellEffects.barrierPriorities.area, strength: (cast, target) => this.strength, usedUp: "never", }; } } onSpellAcross is called for every enabled behavior of a Region that holds a target but not the caster, once per cast, on the active GM's client. barrier counts for the targets inside the Region, for spells cast from outside it. The "from outside" rule is the system's. Its strength(cast, target) gets the incoming cast, so it can depend on who casts: Suppress Lodril's Countermagic only counts against Light, Heat and Sky cultists (RBM p.96). A Region has no effect to use up, so usedUp only decides whether the layer stops the spell. areaRadius(level) returns how far around the caster, in meters, an area spell cast at that level reaches. The cast dialog lights up the squares or hexes in that radius and makes the tokens there the user's targets, the caster included, following the level as it changes. maxTargets(level) returns how many tokens the spell can be cast at, at that level; any number when it's left out. The cast dialog says "at most N targets at this level", and casting at more is refused. The wiki's Turn Undead returns level, one undead per point.

A spell effect that changes rolls, like Berserker or Fanaticism, does it with roll entries. The system calls them from its own "prepare" roll hooks, for every active effect of the spell on the actor who rolls, so what they do shows in the roll dialog. Each entry gets the same arguments as its hook, plus effects: this spell's active effects on that actor. Entry Called from Gets onPrepareAbilityRoll rqg.prepareAbilityRoll item, options, preparation, effects onPrepareCharacteristicRoll rqg.prepareCharacteristicRoll actor, options, preparation, effects onPrepareSpellCast rqg.prepareSpellCast spell, caster, options, preparation, effects onPrepareAttack rqg.prepareAttack weapon, attack, preparation, effects onPrepareDefence rqg.prepareDefence defender, defence, preparation, effects An entry pushes modifiers, for example to options.modifiers, or sets preparation.forbidden to why the roll isn't allowed. Like the prepare hooks, entries run whenever a roll dialog changes, so they must not do anything else. Spells that register the same function are called once with all their effects, like onIncomingSpell. // No parrying while this spell is active const onPrepareDefence = ({ defender, defence, preparation, effects }) => { if (defence.defence === "parry") { preparation.forbidden = `${defender.name} can't parry under ${effects[0].name}.`; } }; registry.register("i.spirit-magic.fanaticism", { onPrepareDefence }, source); Use roll entries rather than your own Hooks.on listeners for spell effects. A behavior is found by rqid, so it runs once even when two language versions of a module are enabled, and a module with a higher priority can replace it.

game.system.api.spellEffects has helpers for common things: summon(scope, actorRqid, options) lets the user place a token of the actor with that rqid, within range and sight of the caster, that goes away when its effect ends. The caster's players observe the token. options.img is the summoning's icon on the token, options.duration overrides the spell's own, and options.footprintMeters ({ w, h }) sets the body's size, like 1×3 m for a medium elemental. giveControl(scope) attaches the spell's effect to the target and, while it lasts, makes the caster's players its owners, as Command (cult spirit) does. Each player gets their previous ownership back when the effect ends, expires or is dispelled; deleting the effect takes the control back. Changing ownership takes the active GM's client, so register the behavior's apply with runAsGm. If the ownership can't be given, the effect is removed and apply resolves to undefined, leaving Apply clickable. pickLocation(scope, { rangeMeters, requireSight }) lets the user click a grid space for a spell that takes a place, within rangeMeters of the caster and in their sight when asked. It resolves to the point, or undefined when cancelled. moveTokenNear(token, point) then moves a token to the free grid space nearest it. list and removeSpellEffects find and remove the spell effects on an actor. The removal filter takes spellRqid, casterActorUuid and maxLevel. castPoints is how strong a cast is against defenses: its magic points plus double its rune points. It is what a barrier is judged against. effectRemovalCost is how many points of Dispel Magic it takes to remove a spell effect. metersToPixels(meters, scene.grid) converts a distance by the scene's grid scale, feet and yards included. The wiki's wards use it for how far their alarm is heard. dealDamage(scope, { formula, armorPoints }) rolls damage with formula and a hit location on the target, shows both rolls in chat like an attack's, and deals the damage once the dice have landed. Pass armorPoints: 0 for damage armor doesn't stop; left out, the location's own armor counts. Run it as the GM (runAsGm) unless the user owns the target. postMagicMissiles(scope, count) posts count more attacks like the one just fired, for Multimissile's magical missiles. Call it from a spell behavior's onMissileFired, which gets { weapon, projectile, attack, effects } when a missile carrying the spell's effect is fired.

Every effect a cast makes carries the cast in effect.system.spell: spellRqid, spellName and spellUuid of the spell, and the cast's caster, castMessageId, level, magicPointsSpent, runePointsSpent and casterSuccessLevel (null when unknown). A spell's area carries the same in its Region behavior's system.spell. list and removeSpellEffects only touch effects that have it.

Hooks.once("rqg.registerSkillBehaviors", (registry) => { const { SuccessLevel } = game.system.api.rolls; registry.register( "i.skill.treat-poison", { apply: async ({ targetActor, targetName }) => { // ... remove the poison effect from targetActor ui.notifications.info(`${targetName}'s poison is treated.`); return { outcome: "resolved" }; }, // Only offer Apply on a success successLevels: [SuccessLevel.Critical, SuccessLevel.Special, SuccessLevel.Success], }, { lang: "en", priority: 10 }, ); }); Skill behaviors work for skills, runes and passions. A skill behavior has these parts: Part When it runs What it returns apply When Apply is clicked. Required { outcome: "resolved" } or nothing successLevels Not run: lists the results Apply is offered for, default all – Compare successLevels with game.system.api.rolls.SuccessLevel. The targets are the tokens the user had targeted when rolling. With no target, the actor who rolled is the target, so First Aid can be used on yourself. apply gets one argument with: skill, the rolled skill, rune or passion item actor, the actor who rolled it targetActor and targetName, the target Apply was clicked for. targetName is the token's own name when the target is a token. successLevel and roll, the result of the roll

To damage the target with rolls shown like an attack's, use spellEffects.dealDamage. To damage or heal it directly, call targetActor.damage({ amount, location, armorPoints }) or targetActor.heal({ location, points, wound }). To change rolls while a spell's effect is active, use roll entries. For rules that don't come from a spell, use the roll hooks.

The wiki module's scripts are the best examples to copy from: scripts/spells/dispel-magic.mjs finds and removes spell effects. scripts/spells/spell-barrier.mjs declares the barrier of Countermagic, Shield and Berserker, and the areaBarrier of the wards. scripts/spells/reflection.mjs is Reflection's onResisted. scripts/spells/elementals.mjs summons with spellEffects.summon. scripts/spells/heal.mjs heals with actor.heal. scripts/spells/disruption.mjs rolls damage and a hit location with spellEffects.dealDamage. scripts/spells/spell-areas.mjs makes Shake Earth, the wards and Sanctify with spellEffects.createArea, onAreaEnter and onSpellAcross. scripts/spells/battle-rage.mjs is Berserker and Fanaticism: roll entries for attack, defence, casting and CON rolls, and an onEnd that leaves the berserker Helpless. scripts/skills/first-aid.mjs asks which wound to treat, then rolls the healing to chat and heals it, or damages the location on a fumble. It uses game.system.api.dialogs.chooseWounds without points, which only picks the wound.

Most fields are stored on the character, and you change them with Foundry's update: await actor.update({ "system.attributes.magicPoints.value": 5 }); A field marked calculated is calculated every time the character is prepared (Foundry recalculates the character's data after any change to it or its items) and is never stored. Writing to it has no lasting effect, because the next calculation overwrites it. To change it, change what it's calculated from: a characteristic, an item, a wound or an effect. The field's description says what goes into it. A field marked effect target isn't stored either, but Active Effects are meant to write to it. These fields are under system.effect. They start at 0 (1 for multipliers) every time the character is prepared, and the calculated values read them. See Changing calculated values with effects. The items have the same kind of fields, see Item data. The JSON Schemas the tables are made from are in the system repository, in src/data-model/json-schemas/generated, if you want to use them in your own tools.

An Active Effect that writes straight to a calculated value is overwritten when the value is calculated. Point the effect at the matching effect target field instead, in ADD mode (MULTIPLY for the fields under effect.multiply): await actor.createEmbeddedDocuments("ActiveEffect", [ { name: "Blessed vigor", changes: [{ key: "system.effect.add.hitPoints.max", mode: 2, value: "2" }], }, ]); actor.system.attributes.hitPoints.max; // 2 more than before The rqid of any item is in item.getFlag("rqg", "documentRqidFlags")?.id, see Rqid. The rest of this page covers what the system works out from the rules, which is not stored on the documents.

A weapon is an item with up to four ways of using it, system.usage.oneHand, offHand, twoHand and missile. Each has stored values like strikeRank, minStrength, minDexterity and the linked skill. The attack chance and whether the character is strong and quick enough come from the skill, the weapon's effects and the rules, so ask the weapon: const spear = actor.items.find((i) => i.name === "Spear" && i.type === "weapon"); const info = spear.system.getUsageInfo("twoHand"); info.totalChance; // the linked skill's chance plus the weapon's effect modifiers info.unusable; // true when the character is below the STR or DEX requirement The result also has skillItem, skillChance, weaponEffectModifier, underMinSTR and underMinDEX. The weapon has to belong to a character. Use rolls.attack to attack with it.

await actor.getCastableSpells() lists all spirit and rune magic the character can cast, their own spells first. It's async because matrix spells are looked up from their rqid. It follows the rules for spells from somewhere else than the character, so use it instead of looking through actor.items when you need to know what the character can cast. Each entry has type ("spiritMagic" or "runeMagic"), name, points and source, which says where the spell comes from: source The spell is known by "own" The character "allied" The character's Allied Spirit, or the priest it's bonded to "boundSpirit" A spirit bound into one of the character's items "matrix" A spell matrix the character has equipped Spells from somewhere else than the character also have sourceName, the name of the spirit or the matrix item. Spirit magic has isVariable, rune magic has isOneUse and the cultId and cultName of the cult it's cast through. To group spells by where they come from, use sourceId rather than sourceName, since two spirits or matrix items can have the same name. It's the same for every spell from one source: the character's uuid for their own spells, the Allied Spirit's uuid, boundSpirit:<itemId>:<spiritUuid> for a bound spirit, or the matrix item's uuid. To find the same spell on another character or in another language, compare rqid, which matrix spells have too. casterUuid is the uuid of the character the list belongs to, who casts the spell when you pass it to the roll functions. Pass an entry to rolls.spiritMagic or rolls.runeMagic to cast it.

actor.getMagicPointSources() lists where the character can draw magic points from, in the order a cast draws from them: the order set in the character's Magic Point Sources window. Each entry has id, type, name, magicPoints (value and max) and uuid: type The source id "self" The character's own magic points "self" "item" An equipped, identified item that stores magic points The item's id "boundSpirit" A spirit bound into one of the character's equipped items boundSpirit:<itemId>:<spiritUuid> "ally" The character's Allied Spirit, or the priest it's bonded to "ally" uuid is the item's uuid for an item, otherwise the actor's. Pass id as the magicPointSource option of rolls.spiritMagic or rolls.runeMagic to draw only from that source. A spell from a bound spirit has the spirit's id as its sourceId, so { magicPointSource: spell.sourceId } casts it with the spirit's own magic points.

A character's hit locations are items of type hitLocation, with their hit points in item.system.hitPoints (see Item data). To let the user add or heal a wound the same way as from the character sheet, open the sheet's dialogs: const { dialogs } = game.system.api; await dialogs.addWound("Head", { actor: token }); // asks for the damage and the armor await dialogs.addWound("Head", { actor: token, damage: 7, subtractArmorPoints: false }); await dialogs.healWounds("Head", { actor: token }); // with the head's wounds picked await dialogs.healWounds(undefined, { actor: token }); // all the character's wounds addWound starts with the given damage, and with the Subtract armor points (subtractArmorPoints) and Apply to total hit points (applyToTotalHp) boxes ticked unless they are false. The user can change them before adding the wound. The hit location is the item, or its name, id, uuid or rqid. Given the item itself, its own actor is used. To damage or heal without a dialog, use actor.damage and actor.heal.

Modules can change and react to rolls with Foundry hooks. Every roll calls three hooks, whether it was started from the character sheet, the hotbar, a macro or another module: a prepare hook, to add modifiers or say why the roll isn't allowed, a pre hook, once just before the roll, to cancel it, an after hook with the finished roll. For a spell effect that changes rolls, use the spell's roll entries instead of listening to these hooks. Prepare the roll Before the roll After the roll rqg.prepareAbilityRoll rqg.preAbilityRoll rqg.abilityRoll rqg.prepareCharacteristicRoll rqg.preCharacteristicRoll rqg.characteristicRoll rqg.prepareReputationRoll rqg.preReputationRoll rqg.reputationRoll rqg.prepareSpellCast rqg.preSpellCast rqg.spellCast rqg.prepareAttack rqg.preAttack rqg.attack rqg.prepareDefence rqg.preDefence rqg.defence The hooks get these arguments: Roll Arguments Skill, rune, passion item, (roll), options, (preparation) Characteristic actor, (roll), options, (preparation) Reputation actor, (roll), options, (preparation) Spirit or rune magic spell, caster, (roll), options, (preparation) Attack weapon, attack, (preparation) Defence defender, defence, (preparation) preparation is only given to the "prepare" hooks, and roll only to the "after" hooks. The hooks run on the client of the user who rolls, or for a defence, the user who submits it: the defender's owner or the GM.

A "prepare" hook runs whenever something changes in the roll dialog, and once more when the roll is made. It can: Add modifiers by pushing to options.modifiers, for example { description: "Blinded", value: -20 }. The dialog includes them in its chance and lists them, and they're shown on the chat card. For an attack or defence, push to attack.rollOptions.modifiers or defence.rollOptions.modifiers. Forbid the roll by setting preparation.forbidden to the reason, for example preparation.forbidden = "Vasana can't parry while prone.". The dialog shows the reason and can't roll. A roll started without the dialog, from a macro or another module, is refused with the reason as a warning. Since it runs many times, a "prepare" hook must not do anything else: no notifications, chat messages or document updates. Those belong in the "pre" and "after" hooks.

A "pre" hook runs once, when the roll is made: after the roll dialog is submitted, or straight away with skipDialog. It can cancel the roll by returning false. Nothing is rolled or posted to chat, and the roll method returns nothing. Listeners are called synchronously, so neither a "prepare" nor a "pre" hook can wait for a dialog or a document update. rqg.prepareSpellCast and rqg.preSpellCast run before the cast is checked, so the spell can still be refused for lack of magic points or rune points afterwards. caster is the actor casting the spell, which can be a different actor from the one that has the spell item: a spell from an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a matrix is cast by the character.

An "after" hook gets the finished roll. Compare roll.successLevel with game.system.api.rolls.SuccessLevel, see Rolls. rqg.abilityRoll and rqg.characteristicRoll run before the experience check, rqg.spellCast after the spell's costs are paid.

An attack is rolled when the defender defends, not when the attacker clicks Attack. So: rqg.prepareAttack runs while the attack dialog is open, with no combatManeuver yet, since the maneuver is the button that's clicked. It runs once more, with the maneuver, when the attack is made. rqg.preAttack and rqg.attack run when the attack is made. rqg.attack means the attack card is posted and the ammunition used, and its attack.chatMessage is that card. The attack has no result yet. rqg.prepareDefence runs for the defence chosen in the defence dialog, but not for "ignore". rqg.preDefence runs before the attack and defence are rolled. rqg.defence is the first point where the attack's result is known. It gets the attackRoll, the defenceRoll (if there was a defence) and the updated chatMessage. The attack argument has the attacker, the target (the actor of the token the user targeted when attacking, if any), the usage ("oneHand", "offHand", "twoHand" or "missile"), the combatManeuver, the projectile (the missile fired, or the weapon itself when thrown) and the rollOptions of the attack roll. The maneuver's name is its key for a maneuver from the list, like "HeadButt", or the name typed on the weapon sheet for any other. Localize a key with RQG.Item.Weapon.combatManeuver.<key> to show it. The defence argument has the attacker, the attackChatMessage, the defence ("parry", "dodge" or "ignore", read only), the parryingWeapon and parryingWeaponUsage, and the rollOptions of the defence roll. To forbid a parry or dodge, a rqg.prepareDefence listener sets preparation.forbidden. The defence dialog shows the reason, and the defender picks another defence. Returning false from rqg.preDefence stops the defence instead, and the attack card keeps waiting for one.

// House rule: -20% on every skill roll while blinded Hooks.on("rqg.prepareAbilityRoll", (item, options) => { if (item.actor?.statuses.has("blind")) { options.modifiers.push({ description: "Blinded", value: -20 }); } }); // House rule: no parrying while prone Hooks.on("rqg.prepareDefence", (defender, defence, preparation) => { if (defence.defence === "parry" && defender.statuses.has("prone")) { preparation.forbidden = `${defender.name} is prone and can't parry.`; } }); // Post a message when someone fumbles a characteristic roll Hooks.on("rqg.characteristicRoll", (actor, roll, options) => { if (roll.successLevel === game.system.api.rolls.SuccessLevel.Fumble) { ChatMessage.create({ content: `${actor.name} fumbled ${options.characteristicName}!` }); } });

documents.t: When the RQG system is updated, the first GM to open the world is guided through a world migration that brings old data up to date with the new version. The functions in game.system.api.maintenance let a GM run the steps of that migration by hand, for example to clean up after importing old content into a world that has already been migrated. All of them only work for a GM; for anyone else they throw an error. Make a backup of the world before running them.

When a GM opens a world that was last used with an older version of the system, these steps run in order: Repair invalid data – the Data Model Repair dialog lists actors and items that Foundry can't load because some value is no longer valid, and lets you fix them. Foundry is reloaded afterwards if anything was changed. Add missing RQG ids – the RQID batch editor asks for rqids on skills, rune magic, spirit magic, runes and cults that don't have one. The system needs them, for example to connect weapons to their skills. See RQG System ID (rqid). Migrate the world – after you confirm, actors, items, active effects and unlinked tokens in the world are updated, as well as those in compendiums from modules and the world. The system's own compendiums are skipped since they already ship updated. A report journal entry lists what was changed, and any warnings or errors. If the migration finishes without errors the world is marked as migrated, so it doesn't run again.
documents.s: What happens when the system is updated

documents.t: await game.system.api.maintenance.openDataModelRepairDialog(); Looks through the world's actors and items for documents Foundry can't load, and opens a dialog to fix them. Invalid values can be reset, and documents with a type that no longer exists can be deleted. Afterwards it asks if you want to reload Foundry, which is needed for the changes to take effect. If nothing is wrong you just get a notification saying so.

// Check the same item types as the world migration does await game.system.api.maintenance.openRqidBatchEditor(); // Only check skills and passions await game.system.api.maintenance.openRqidBatchEditor("skill", "passion"); Finds items without an rqid, in the world and in compendiums, and opens an editor where you can give them one. Items with the same name are grouped so they get the same rqid. One editor opens per item type that has items missing an rqid. An item type that doesn't exist, like "skil", throws an error that lists the valid ones.

// What would the system's own migrations change in this world? Nothing is written. const report = await game.system.api.maintenance.applyWorldMigrations({ system: true, dryRun: true, }); console.log(`${report.documents.length} documents would change, ${report.errorCount} errors`); Runs migrations over the world's actors, items and scenes with unlinked tokens and, if you ask for it, compendiums. It is safe to run more than once, since the migrations only change data that still needs it. Nothing is migrated unless you ask for it: pass system: true for the system's own migrations, your own migrations (see below), or both. Option What it does system Also run the system's own migrations, the same as when the system is updated. Default false. items A list of your own item migrations. actors A list of your own actor migrations. activeEffects A list of your own active effect migrations. They run on active effects in compendiums. dryRun Work out and report what would change without changing anything. Default false. scope What to include besides the world: "world" (default) no compendium, "all" every compendium except the system's, or a list of compendium ids like ["world.my-items"]. report Write the report to the migration journal, like the automatic migration does. Default true, false for a dry run. Compendiums that belong to the system are never migrated. When a compendium is migrated it is unlocked for the run and locked again afterwards. A compendium that doesn't exist in scope throws an error before anything runs.

The function returns a report, which is also what ends up in the journal: { dryRun: true, errorCount: 0, warningCount: 0, inspected: { worldActorsInspected: 149, worldItemsInspected: 580, /* ... */ }, documents: [ { kind: "Item", uuid: "Item.abc123", name: "Lore", migration: "renameLocalLore", // the migrations that changed it changes: [{ path: "name", from: "Lore (Local)", to: "Local Lore" }], hiddenChangeCount: 0, // changes that were too many to list }, ], errors: [{ message: "Failed system migration for Item …", uuid: "Item.def456" }], } from and to are the values as text. When the change is to an item an actor owns, kind is "Actor" and each path starts with the item's name and ::, like Spirit Combat :: system.specialization. With report: true the report is also added to the migration journal. A dry run doesn't write one unless you pass report: true, and then it is labelled "Dry run".

A dry run changes nothing, so later steps don't see what earlier steps would have done. The changes for the unlinked tokens in a scene, for example, are worked out on top of the original world actors, not the migrated ones. A dry run can therefore list changes a real run wouldn't make. It never leaves out a change a real run would make.
