documents.t: caution Custom migrations change every matching document the run reaches. Do a dry run first, and test on a copy of the world. Module developers and technically minded GMs can pass their own migration functions. They run after the system's own, if you also pass system: true. A migration is an async function that gets the document and returns the update data for it, or nothing to leave it unchanged. The same shape is used for items (items), actors (actors) and active effects (activeEffects). This example renames the skill "Lore (Local)" to "Local Lore" everywhere in the world, and doesn't run any of the system's migrations: const renameLocalLore = async (item) => item.type === "skill" && item.name === "Lore (Local)" ? { name: "Local Lore" } : undefined; // Look first const dry = await game.system.api.maintenance.applyWorldMigrations({ items: [renameLocalLore], dryRun: true, }); console.table(dry.documents.map((d) => ({ name: d.name, changes: d.changes.length }))); // Then do it await game.system.api.maintenance.applyWorldMigrations({ items: [renameLocalLore] }); The name of the function is shown as the migration in the report, so give it a descriptive one.

The functions in game.system.api.rolls do the same rolls as clicking on the character sheet. By default they open the normal roll dialog, where the player can add modifiers before rolling. With skipDialog: true the roll is made straight away instead, like double-clicking on the sheet. The function then returns the roll, so a macro can check the result with roll.successLevel. Compare it with game.system.api.rolls.SuccessLevel: { Critical: 0, Special: 1, Success: 2, Failure: 3, Fumble: 4 }. A lower number is a better result, so roll.successLevel <= SuccessLevel.Success means the roll succeeded. Experience checks, magic point and rune point costs are handled the same way as when rolling from the sheet.

Function Rolls ability(item, options) A skill, rune or passion characteristic(name, options) A characteristic roll, ×5 by default reputation(options) The character's Reputation attack(weapon, { actor, usage }) Opens the attack dialog for a weapon. It always uses the dialog spiritMagic(spell, options) Casts a spirit magic spell runeMagic(spell, options) Casts a rune magic spell For characteristic the name is one of "strength", "constitution", "size", "dexterity", "intelligence", "power" or "charisma". For attack, usage picks how the weapon is used: "oneHand", "offHand", "twoHand" or "missile". The choice is remembered on the weapon, just like when it's changed in the attack dialog. The spell functions can also cast spells the character doesn't have as an item: spells known through an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a spell matrix. Get those from await actor.getCastableSpells() and pass one of them as the spell. It's cast by the character whose list it came from, with that character's token, and an actor option naming anyone else is an error.

All options are optional. Option Used by Meaning actor all Who rolls, see Pointing at actors and items skipDialog all but attack Roll at once and return the roll modifiers all but attack A list of modifiers like [{ description: "Darkness", value: -20 }] rollMode all but attack Foundry roll mode, for example "gm" difficulty characteristic What to multiply the characteristic with, 5 by default levelUsed spells Points to cast with, defaults to the spell's points. Only variable spirit magic can use fewer, down to 1, and only stackable rune magic more magicPointBoost spells Extra magic points to boost the spell with magicPointSource spells Where magic points are drawn from: "auto" (the default) follows the character's draw order, or the id of one of actor.getMagicPointSources() The spell dialogs start with the given levelUsed, magicPointBoost, magicPointSource and rollMode, and the player can change them. levelUsed is only used for spells cast at a chosen level, variable spirit magic and stackable rune magic. A magicPointSource that isn't one of the character's sources is an error from these functions. For the other rolls, rollMode and difficulty are only used together with skipDialog, in the dialog the player picks them. modifiers are only used together with skipDialog too, except for ability: there they are added as fixed modifiers that the player can't change. They aren't shown as fields in the dialog, but they are included in the target chance, listed when hovering it, and shown on the chat card.

const api = game.system.api; // Open the roll dialog for Scan, for the selected token await api.rolls.ability("Scan"); // Roll Dodge for a specific token without a dialog, and check the result const roll = await api.rolls.ability("Dodge", { actor: token, skipDialog: true }); if (roll.successLevel <= api.rolls.SuccessLevel.Success) { ui.notifications.info("Dodged!"); } // Cast Bladesharp 2 await api.rolls.spiritMagic("Bladesharp", { skipDialog: true, levelUsed: 2 }); A spell that can't be cast, for example because there aren't enough magic points, shows a warning and returns nothing.

A module that already has the actor or item can call the roll methods on it directly, without looking it up by name. The functions above are thin wrappers around these: Method Rolls item.roll(options) A skill, rune or passion actor.rollCharacteristic(name, options) A characteristic, with difficulty like characteristic actor.rollReputation(options) The character's Reputation item.cast(options) A spirit or rune magic spell, cast by the actor that has it actor.castSpell(spell, options) A spirit or rune magic spell, cast by this actor item.attack({ usage }) Opens the attack dialog for a weapon They take the same options as the functions, except actor. Pass token instead to choose which of the actor's tokens is the speaker on the chat card. Leaving it out uses the actor's own token, if it has one. Use actor.castSpell for a spell the actor knows through an Allied Spirit, a bound spirit or a matrix: the spell item belongs to the spirit or the matrix, but actor is the caster who spends the magic points. Rune magic also takes runePointSource (which cult's rune points to spend) and usedRuneId (which rune to roll), and the rune magic dialog starts with them. Both kinds take magicPointSource. // In a module: roll the Constitution ×3 of a combatant's token without a dialog const roll = await combatant.actor.rollCharacteristic("constitution", { token: combatant.token, difficulty: 3, skipDialog: true, }); The roll hooks run for every roll, wherever it was started from.

documents.t: await actor.addSpellEffect({ token }) opens the same Add a Spell Effect dialog as the + in the token HUD's status palette. The user searches for a spell, sets its level and clicks Add, and the spell's effect goes on the actor as if someone else had cast it, or the actor itself when "Cast by" is ticked. The actor's protective spells, like Countermagic, can stop it as they would a cast. It resolves true when the actor's effects changed and false when they didn't, for example when the dialog was closed. A spell that was stopped can still change the effects, by using up a protective spell or cancelling one already on the actor, and then resolves true too. token is the target token. The dialog's title names it, and protective spell areas on the scene see where it stands. Leaving it out uses the actor's own token, if it has one. Anyone who owns the actor can use it, like the + in the token HUD. For an actor the user doesn't own it shows a warning and resolves false without opening the dialog. // In a module: add a spell effect to the selected token, then refresh the module's own HUD const token = canvas.tokens.controlled[0]?.document; if (token && (await token.actor.addSpellEffect({ token }))) { refreshMyHud(); }

documents.t: The RQG System manages content in different languages and different compendiums or in the world by using a RQG System ID or "rqid". The id's are stored as flags on documents under the "rqg" scope as an object "documentRqidFlags" containing id, lang & priority properties. A rqid is not a unique id, instead it defines what "kind" a document is. The purpose is to let different versions of the same document coexist so the "best" version can be used. A "kind" can be something like a specific skill like "Dodge", or a description of a specific spell. It also defines what language the document is written in, and it has a priority that ranks documents with the same id and language (higher is better). An advantage of using rqid for links between documents is that the risk of broken links are greatly reduced, compared to linking documents using the Foundry Uuid. If a link is broken you just need to either make sure a document matching the requested rqid once again is available in your world or in a compendium, or change the link to some other rqid that exists. See Current usage in the system for details on what it's currently used for. If you want to link to a specific instance of a document you should use the Foundry uuid instead.

A normal rqid comes in 3 parts separated by dots . like this: i.skill.fast-talk. It should be all lower case letters without any spaces. The first part is an abbreviated document type, see below. It supports many different document types, but the system only uses links to items, journals and Active Effects so far. Document type abbreviation table Foundry Document Type a Actor ae ActiveEffect (only found in compendium packs) c Cards i Item je JournalEntry jp JournalEntryPage (Only allowed as embedded in JournalEntry) m Macro p Playlist rt RollTable s Scene The second part is the document subtype if there is any. In RQG there are a number of item types like skill, hit-location and rune etc. The third part is usually related to the name of the document in english. If it is a journal entry for example is describing the spell bladesharp (rqid i.spirit-magic.bladesharp), it can be called je..bladesharp, and the spell's effect can be called ae..bladesharp rqids for embedded documents There is also a possibility to link to a document that is embedded. This is mostly useful for adding a link to a journal entry page inside a journal entry. The rqid for that can look like this je..spells.jp..ignite where the first section (je..spells) defines what document it is, and the appended section (jp..ignite) defines what embedded document to find inside that document.

The available documents matching "rqid" and "lang" will be searched, and it will return the one with the highest priority. This allows later RQG content packs to override older information. The GM can also use this to create compendium packs with documents that override the ones provided by the system. A search for a document can look like this: await game.system.api.rqid.fromRqid("i.skill.act", "es") to find the best available act skill in Spanish. The priorities are: The id has to match the query The language - either the one specified in the query, the world language (as in the setting) or the fallback language (english) The priority value - the highest priority wins, whether the document is in the world or in a compendium The found document is in the world - if a world document and a compendium document have the same priority, the world document is used Active Effects have no world collection, so an ae rqid is only found in compendium packs. Examples of priorities and search results A spell item has a rqid link je..befuddle to a journal entry that describes that spell. When a player clicks the link a search is done to find the best match. Suppose these journal entries describing some spirit magic spells exist: rqid: je..befuddle, language: en, priority: 0 (from the wiki module) rqid: je..befuddle, language: en, priority: 1000 (from a higher priority english module) rqid: je..befuddle, language: es, priority: 0 (from a custom "translation to Spanish" module) rqid: je..demoralize, language: en, priority: 0 (from the wiki module) rqid: je..demoralize, language: en, priority: 1000 (from a higher priority english module) A search for fromRqid("je..befuddle", "en") would return journal entry 2, since that has the highest priority. A search for fromRqid("je..befuddle", "es") would return journal entry 3 even though journal entry 2 has a higher priority since the language is more important than the priority. A search for fromRqid("je..demoralize", "es") would return journal entry 5 since there is no spanish version with that rqid, but the fallback language is english, and journal entry 5 has a higher priority compared to journal entry 4.

A number of RQG items have a "rqidLink" to a journal entry description. The advantage of this is that the "best" version will be opened. For example if you only have the wiki module installed then that (limited) description will be opened. If you in the future install a premium module that contains a more elaborated description with the same rqid, but higher priority, then that will be opened instead. This can also be used to change what language version is opened, since the world language setting is tried first. If no description is found in that language the english version is opened (if that exists). For reference, these RQG items that have a rqid description link Cult Rune Rune Magic Spirit Magic discussion Removing the world language setting and relying on the user language is probably a bad idea since it could make it hard to know what the players actually will see. For example a game played in Spanish where one player has selected Swedish as the Foundry language would mean that the Swedish user would get the default English versions of any linked journal entries - and they might not match the journals the GM has prepared. I think it's natural that a game is played in one language (matching the world language setting) and that all players see the documents in that language. Then again you could argue that since there is a user language setting in Foundry, and since that will affect the Foundry interface language, it might make sense to use that instead.

documents.t: There are a few skills that need special handling, and these are identified by the system by looking at the rqid of the skills. This allows the name of these skills to be translated into any language. dodge: i.skill.dodge, jump: i.skill.jump, worship: i.skill.worship, moveQuietly: i.skill.move-quietly, spiritCombat: i.skill.spirit-combat, The Magic condition rune (i.rune.magic-condition) is identified the same way.

Armor items needs to specify what hit locations they protect. This is accomplished by a list of rqids for hit location items. When a piece of armor is embedded in an actor and equipped, the embedded hit location items that matches the rqids in the armor item is found and the protection is applied. Note that this usage of rqid does not use the language, instead it only searches for the rqids in the embedded items of the actor using the actor.getBestEmbeddedDocumentByRqid(rqid) function on the RqgActor class. The list of available hit-locations is indexed at startup, see green box further down.

documents.t: Rune Magic spells have a list of rune rqids to identify what runes they can be cast with. When the spell is cast the rqids are used to find the rune items that are embedded in the actor to figure out success chances. The list of available runes is indexed at startup, see green box further down.

documents.t: danger Support for sorcery is still alpha level and will change, see Sorcery. The list of available runes is indexed at startup, see green box further down.

Runes use rqid to define what the minor and opposite runes are for a particular rune. Currently only the "opposite" rune link is used for finding what other Power rune to adjust when a Power runes chance is adjusted. The list of available runes is indexed at startup, see green box further down.

An Active Effect on an actor can change a value on one of the actor's embedded items, not just on the actor itself. Such a change has an "Attribute Key" that starts with @, followed by which items to change, a :, and the path of the item's value: Key Changes @<rqid>:system.<path> The actor's best embedded item with that rqid @~<regex>:system.<path> Every embedded item whose rqid matches the regular expression @.:system.<path> The item the effect is on (only for an effect that belongs to an item) The change types are Foundry's normal ones: Add, Multiply, Override, Upgrade and Downgrade. Custom can't be used with an @ key. A regular expression can't contain a :, and has no flags. Keys that don't start with @ are normal Foundry keys and work exactly as in Foundry, including core's token. keys, which change the actor's tokens. For example, token.light.dim makes the token give off light. A key that can't be used, such as an rqid the actor has no item for, shows the GM a warning. The path is the path to the item system property that should be changed. It is not obvious how to find this, but looking at the code for the item type in question can help. For example looking at the data models at https://github.com/sun-dragon-cult/fvtt-system-rqg/tree/main/src/data-model/item-data can give a hint of what to write. Another way to find the path, especially for the actor, is to mark a token in a scene in Chrome, open the developer tools (press F12) and in the console type _token.actor.system and see what comes out. Bonus values: values under system.effect.add are bonuses that are added to a value the system calculates. They start at 0 and aren't saved, so use them with Add (or Upgrade / Downgrade). Multiply and Override show a warning, since they make no sense for a bonus. On the actor: system.effect.add.magicPoints.max, system.effect.add.hitPoints.max and system.effect.add.skillCategoryModifiers.<category> (agility, communication, knowledge, magic, manipulation, perception, stealth, meleeWeapons, missileWeapons, shields, naturalWeapons, otherSkills) On a weapon: system.effect.add.melee.attack, .parry and .damage, and the same for missile Spell level: in an effect that comes from a spell, @level in the value is the level the spell was cast at, for example @level * 5. Active Effect Examples Climb skill bonus: ADD @i.skill.climb:system.baseChance, value 10 Natural armor on every hit location: ADD @~^i\.hit-location\.:system.naturalAp, value 2 Bladesharp on the weapon it's cast on: ADD @.:system.effect.add.melee.attack, value @level * 5 Magic point bonus: ADD system.effect.add.magicPoints.max, value 2 (no rqid) Agility skills bonus: ADD system.effect.add.skillCategoryModifiers.agility, value 5 (no rqid) Strength: ADD system.characteristics.strength.value, value 8 (no rqid). Values derived from STR, like damage bonus, follow. Most other actor attributes are derived from characteristics, so an effect on them is overwritten. Changed in 6.2.0 Before RQG 6.2.0 a change to an item used a Custom key without the @, like i.hit-location.head:system.naturalAp. The world migration rewrites these to the @ form on Add, and one that is left, for example in a module's compendium, shows the GM a warning and does nothing. The old keys system.attributes.magicPoints.max and system.attributes.hitPoints.max are migrated to their system.effect.add versions.

Weapons are linked to which skills they use for each usage (like one handed, two handed or missile). The links use rqid and when a weapon is embedded, first a check if a skill matching the rqid is already embedded, and if not a search for the best skill is done and that one is embedded on the actor. When a weapon is used the rqid is used to find the embedded skill to roll against.

Cults have rqid links to both what runes the cult has and what common rune magic spells you should get when joining the cult. The linked common rune spells are embedded in the actor when the cult item is embedded in the actor. If the spell is not already embedded in the actor, a search for the best version of the linked spells is done using the world language. On the actor sheet these spells have a marking, and to know which spells gets marks is compares the rqid to that list. When casting rune magic spells the runes to cast with is searched in the actor by using rqid.

A spell that has an effect links to it with an Active Effect rqid in its Effect field (effectRqidLink), for example ae..bladesharp. When the spell takes effect, the best version of that effect is copied onto the target, so a higher priority module can replace an effect the same way it replaces a description. The effect's incompatible spells are a list of spell rqids, like i.spirit-magic.fireblade, that can't be on the same target at the same time. Recasting a spell is recognised by the spell's rqid, so a spell without an rqid is never treated as the same spell as another. The token HUD's + lists the best version of each compendium spell that has an effect, in the world language where possible.

Rqid links only store the rqid. The name shown on a link is the name of the document it finds, searched the same way as when the link is opened, in the language of the world. When a module adds a better version or a translation, every link shows its name, and lists of links are sorted by the names shown. A link that finds no document shows its rqid instead, with a warning sign and a red dashed border, like a broken Foundry link. Usually the module that has the document isn't active, or the rqid is misspelled. Runes and hit location items in compendiums are indexed at startup (usage 3-5) When (re)loading the browser all compendiums containing all rune and hit location items are indexed and lists of all unique runes / hit locations that are available are compiled. The world language is used to select what language should be part of the list, and the highest priority item that matched the world language for each rqid is kept. These lists are used to populate dropdowns of available runes / hit locations. Please note that world runes / hit locations are not part of this indexing, so if you want to add more runes or hit locations than are provided by the wiki module, then you need to put the extra items in a compendium pack of your own.

When a macro or module, needs a specific document, for example a Broadsword or the journal entry describing dwarves, it can call await game.system.api.rqid.fromRqid("i.weapon.broadsword", "es"), where the first parameter is the invariant rqid, and the second parameter is the requested language code. If you do not include a language code, it will use the language from the setting "world language" when searching for the document. If the document is not available in the requested language it will try to find it in English as a fallback before giving up. To show a link's name, game.system.api.rqid.nameFromRqid("i.skill.dance") returns the name of the best match without loading the document, or undefined when nothing matches. Not Yet Implemented - TODO ⚠️ Changing language in a world​ Actors and items embedded in an actor will not be changed even if you switch language in the world language setting, or activate a module that contains higher priority versions of the same items. It should be possible to "migrate" a world to a different language. Or change an English module to use for example Spanish item names. It's probably only reasonable to let such a migration affect world items? Possible ways this could be done: A script that goes through all world actors and the embedded items, and for each item overwrites the name and possibly other properties from the item with the same rqid, but matching the world language. A way to migrate a specific actor, maybe with an "upgrade" button on the actor sheet in edit mode that searches for the best version of each embedded item and overwrites selected properties from there.

Search for "RuneQuest Glorantha" in the Foundry VTT Install System search box and press "Install" button. You will also need the "Wiki content for the RQG system" module. When installing the system, it will ask if you want to install the recommended modules as well. Allow this and when you have created your world activate the "Wiki content for the RQG system" module.

or NPC, Monster or Ghost, etc A newly created Foundry actor contains very little, and tabs that have no corresponding items are not shown on the character sheet (making it look very empty). To see examples of how finished actors can look like you can have a peek in the Wiki Bestiary folder. tip The easiest way to create a new actor is to start from a template. In Foundry's Create Actor dialog, set Start from to Choose template... and pick one from the list. The wiki module provides templates for adventurers, like "Human (Base)", "Human (Sartarite)" and "Mostali (Dwarf)", and for creatures, like animals, chaos monsters, elementals, mounts and spirits. You can search the list by name and filter it by class (human, elder race, animal, chaos, ...), role (such as adventurer) and species. Each entry shows where the template comes from, and its language and priority. The new actor is a copy of the template with all its items. Actors in your world or your own compendiums are listed too when they are tagged as templates, with the role:template tag in their flags.rqg.tags. There is no field for it on the actor sheet yet. If you want to start from a freshly created actor to be able to maximise the customisation, these are the steps.

The compendium "Hit Locations/Humanoids" contain the normal humanoid hitlocations. Drag these to the actor. A tip here is to drag the entire compendium to the actor at once instead of dragging each individual hitlocation from the compendium by its own. There are other compendiums with hitlocations for other body types. See Hit Location for details about this item type.

The compendium "Runes/Runes(Player Character)" contains all the runes from the RQG character sheet. Drag them to the actor in the same way as the hitlocations. If you want to choose from the full set of runes present in the Chaosium Wiki then have a look in the "Runes/Runes (All)" compendium. More info about this item type can be found here Rune item.

The compendium "Skills & Passions/Skills" contain skills. Drag all (or a subset) of those skills to the character. Please note that this compendium contains all skills, including specialised skills that not all actors have. A better base selection of skills is in the Human (Base) actor (see tip further up). Skill item contains more info bout this item type.

There is a set of cults predefined - look in the compendium "Cults & Magic/Cults" and drag the cult of your choice to let the adventurer join a cult. See Cult Item for detailed info about these items.

Again there is a compendium with Rune Magic spells that can be found at "Cults & Magic/Rune Magic Spells" that you can drag to the actor. More detailed info about this kind of item can be found at Rune Magic Spell Item

You might already guess how to do this... Look for the "Cults & Magic/Spirit Magic Spells" compendium and drag the ones you want to the actor. More info about this item type can be found at Spirit Magic Spell Item
Create a Passion item - or use one of the provided Passions in the "Skills & Passions/Passions" compendium and drag it to the character sheet. Passion Item contains more detailed info.

Armor is its own item type, and you can find ready-made armor items at "Equipment/Armor". To actually be protected you need to equip the armor on the Gear Tab. The equipped icon looks like this and more detailed info about this item type can be found at Armor Item. If you are creating a creature that has natural armor you should look at Hit Location Item where that can be specified.

Weapons are the most complex item type, but you can find most weapons you need in the "Equipment/Weapons" compendium. More details about this item type can be found in Weapon Item. To be able to use the weapon you've dragged to your actor you need to equip it . Arrows and other ammunition is also weapon items.

There are three types of Gear Items in the "Equipment/Gear" compendium, currency gear like Lunar and Wheels, that will show up in the currency table on the Gear Tab, consumable gear with quantity that will show up in the consumable table, and unique gear that will show up in the gear table. Some gear items can also contain other items. That is handled with the Location system.

RuneQuest measures everything in meters: a movement unit (MOV) is 3 meters, and spell ranges and areas are given in meters. The system sets new scenes to 1.5 meters per grid space. Keep the scene's grid units in meters, as the movement ruler and spell areas count in them.

All three work: Hexes are the common choice for RuneQuest maps. Distance is counted hex by hex. Squares need one Foundry setting to match the rules, see below. Gridless scenes measure straight lines in meters. Spell areas then show as plain circles instead of lit-up spaces, and nothing snaps to a grid.

Foundry's default, Equidistant, counts a diagonal step as one space, the same as a straight one. A human with MOV 8 (24 meters) could then move 16 squares diagonally, about 34 meters. Spell areas always measure true distance, so a 3 meter Harmony wouldn't reach the squares the ruler calls 3 meters away diagonally. Set Configure Settings → Core → Grid Diagonals to Exact. A diagonal step then counts as about 2.1 meters, which matches the rules, and the movement ruler and spell areas agree. It's a world setting, so it covers every scene. The system doesn't change it for you, since that would change movement in worlds already in play.

When a token in combat is dragged, its ruler is colored by how far it moves, from its MOV: Green up to half its movement, when it can still attack. Yellow up to its full movement. Orange beyond its full movement. Red beyond its sprint, when the optional sprint rule is on: set Sprint Range Multiplier in the system's token ruler settings.

This page follows a spell from the cast dialog to the effect on its target, in the order the system handles it. Spirit magic and Rune magic go the same way. What the spell then does is covered on Spells.

The dialog shows the caster, the targets, the level and any magic points to boost the spell with. The level is at least 1 and a boost at least 0. Targets are the tokens you have targeted when you press Cast. Spells centered on the caster, like Harmony and Inviolable, take everyone within their radius instead, the caster included, whatever is targeted. The dialog says how far that is, and the squares or hexes it covers are lit up on the scene, growing and shrinking with the level. Tokens hidden from the caster's player aren't included; the GM handles those. Spells resisted by a single target take one target, picked in the dialog's dropdown: the tokens you can see, nearest first, or "(yourself)". Spells cast at a creature, spirit, hit location or another spell have the same dropdown. A spell is cast at one target, unless it says otherwise. Casting at more is refused. Spells on the caster and summons, like Axe Trance or Summon Earth Elemental, always go on the caster, whatever is targeted. With nothing targeted, a spell that can't be resisted (like Protection), or one that can only be on its caster or their weapon (like Bladesharp), goes on the caster. A spell that can be resisted gets a pending "No target" row for the GM to rule on. Some spells reach more targets, like Turn Undead, one undead per point, or Oath, one participant per point. The dialog says how many, and casting at more is refused.

The cast card shows the roll and the points spent. If the cast fails, no target is affected and nothing else happens. A spell's strength against defenses is its points: magic points as they are, Rune points double, plus any boost. A 2-point Rune spell boosted with 1 magic point has strength 5.

A spell cast from outside a spell area at a target inside it crosses the area's boundary, and the area can react, once per cast: A ward (Warding or Create Market) sounds its alarm, heard by the GM and the players with tokens within 500 m. Any Region a module has made can react to a spell cast across it in the same way. Sanctify alerts its caster that a spell crossed in. The caster's players aren't told whose; the GM is. This happens whether the spell then gets through or not.

Before anyone resists, each target's protective spells meet the spell, in layers from the outside in. The first one that stops it settles that target: its row on the card reads "No effect", stopped by a protective spell, and it gets no resistance roll. The card doesn't say which spell stopped it. Layer Stops the spell when its strength is… Used up? Ward at most the ward's Countermagic + 1 Never. A spell it stops never reaches the target's own defenses. Countermagic 2 or more below it, or within 1 point of it Within 1 point, both are gone. A spell 2 or more points stronger breaks it. Shield at most twice its points Never. The layers are met in a row, each at the spell's full strength: a spell that gets through one meets the next undiminished. Layers of the same kind don't stack, only the strongest counts. That is why Berserker, which counts as Countermagic 2, or 4 against a chaotic caster, doesn't add to a Countermagic spell. A ward only protects non-hostile tokens inside it, against spells from outside it. A target's own defenses don't stop a spell it casts on itself, and spells marked Gets through Countermagic and Shield, like Dismiss Magic, pass them all. Protective spells and Regions from other modules take part the same way, each at the position its module gave it. A module's layer can sit between the ones above, so check the module's own description when a spell is stopped somewhere unexpected. Nothing keeps a module from putting an inner defense outside a ward; the GM can see it, and change it. Casting order. The rules agree that Countermagic is met before Shield, but the RBM Q&A on Countermagic layers protective spells in the order they were cast, outward from the body. RQG always meets Countermagic first, the reading of the Core Q&A and the RBM Q&A on Shield, and it has no setting for the other. If your table plays by casting order, rule it yourself when it matters. This works for every spell, including ones with no automation at all.

What happens next depends on the spell's Resisted By field: Resisted By What happens None The spell takes effect on every target it reached. Resistance roll (single target) The target's owner gets a resistance request: the caster's POW against the target's POW. Resistance roll, per target The same, one request per target, like Turn Undead. Resistance roll, whole area The caster makes one roll, and the card says which POW it affects, like "affects POW 15 or lower". Every target is settled from that at once. Spirit combat The GM rules each target won or lost on the cast card, until spirit combat itself is automated. A target may also accept the spell instead of resisting. Casting on yourself counts as accepting. No POW. A side without POW uses its current magic points instead, the caster as well as the target (RBM p.6). Undead are the usual case, which is why Turn Undead is resisted with magic points. An empty POW and a POW of 0 both count as no POW: a living creature dies when its POW reaches 0, so leave POW empty on a creature that has none. A target with neither POW nor magic points can't resist: its card says so and the spell takes effect. A Manual side in a resistance roll keeps the value and label you type. Reflection acts when the target's resistance holds, by roll or by the GM's ruling: if its Reflection is strong enough (each point turns back 2 points of spirit magic or 1 Rune point), the spell goes back at its caster, and the card says so. A stronger spell isn't reflected, and the Reflection stays. On its way back the spell meets the caster's own protective spells, as in step 4; if they stop it, the card reads "No effect" and nobody rolls. Otherwise the caster gets a resistance request: their POW when they cast it against their POW now. A spell is only reflected once, even if the caster has Reflection too.

Each target the spell takes effect on gets an Apply button on the card, for that target's owner. What it does depends on the spell: it puts the spell's effect on the target, or runs the spell's behavior, see Spells. A spell with neither has no Apply button; the GM and players handle the effect by hand. On Apply, the spells already on the target have their say: A spell the target already has active has no effect, or replaces it if the new casting is stronger, as the world setting Recast Spells Take Effect decides, see Recasting and incompatible spells. Some spells can't share a target, and calming spells like Harmony remove weaker rage spells like Fanaticism, or keep them from taking hold.

A spell's effect shows on the token. Temporal spells last their duration. Spells that affect a place, like Shake Earth, Warding or Sanctify, make a scene Region instead. The caster places it, snapped to the grid, and the squares or hexes it will cover light up as it moves: Ranged spells must lie wholly within range, centered on a point the caster can see. The scene is dimmed outside what the caster's token can see within range. For a point the caster perceives by magic, the GM places it in sight and then drags the Region where it belongs. Rituals can be placed anywhere, as a ritual is held where its area is. A ward is placed by clicking its four wands. The GM and the caster's players see the area; a spell like Mist Cloud is seen by everyone. The area puts its effect on the tokens inside it and takes it off those who leave, and the GM can move or delete it like any Region. Areas measure in meters; see Setting Up Scenes for the grid settings that match them.

A spell ends when its duration runs out, or when its effect is deleted: by Dispel or Dismiss Magic, by the GM, or used up, like Countermagic that stopped a spell within 1 point of it. Deleting a spell area's Region on the scene ends that spell too. When it ends: The spell's own end runs, if it has one. A Berserker collapses helpless, and the chat says so. A summoned creature leaves: its token is removed from the scene. A spell area is removed from the scene, and everyone inside loses its effect. An expired effect is deleted from the token. Nothing comes back when a spell ends: a weaker casting of the same spell that didn't take hold isn't waiting underneath. A spell runs out when the game time or the combat moves past its duration. Foundry checks that, and the system ends the spell, on the GM's client, so it needs a GM connected.

A hidden cast (blind or private) keeps the spell's name from the target's player, even when it is reflected. Ward alarms and Sanctify alerts don't name who crossed or who cast at whom to players. The GM gets the names. Why a spell was stopped on Apply, by a spell already on the target, is only shown to that target's owners.

To create a Cult, just create a cult item and give it a name and tagline. The cult should also have a number of runes associated with it and there is a dropdown to select runes from the available runes. To add another rune just keep selecting runes in the empty dropdown. To remove a rune, delete the text in the input field. If you drag the cult item to an actor, it will end up under the Rune Magic Tab

The wiki module gives the spells it ships with real effects: Apply puts a Bladesharp on a weapon, Dispel Magic removes spells, Summon Earth Elemental places a token. A spell that isn't in the wiki module, for example one from the Red Book of Magic or one you made up, keeps working like it always did. It is cast, the points are spent and the GM rules on the result by hand. This page shows how to give such a spell an effect of its own. Which way to go depends on what the spell should do: The spell should… Use Add a bonus, change a value, or just show that it's active until it ends An effect template, no code Remove other spells, summon, stop other spells, or anything that is logic A behavior in a module Work like a wiki spell but with your own change A copy of the wiki spell

An effect template is an Active Effect that lives in a compendium. The spell links to it, and Apply puts a copy on the target. You do this once per spell. It needs four things: a compendium for effects, the effect, an rqid on the effect, and the link from the spell.

In the Compendium Packs tab, click Create Compendium, choose the document type Active Effect, and give it a name. A world compendium is fine, you don't need a module. Effects can only be found by their rqid in a compendium, which is why they can't just be dropped in the world.
documents.s: 1. Make a compendium for your effects

documents.t: An effect needs an rqid, like ae..thunderfist, so that spells can link to it. The effect sheet has no rqid button yet, so the easiest way is a macro. Create a Script macro, adapt it and run it as the GM: const pack = game.packs.get("world.my-spell-effects"); // the compendium from step 1 await ActiveEffect.create( { name: "Thunderfist", img: "icons/svg/lightning.svg", type: "base", system: { // +5 to attack per level of the spell, on the weapon the spell is cast on changes: [{ key: "@.:system.effect.add.melee.attack", type: "add", value: "@level * 5" }], }, flags: { rqg: { documentRqidFlags: { id: "ae..thunderfist", lang: "en", priority: 0 } } }, }, { pack: pack.collection }, ); The changes are the same as on any Active Effect. @level is the level the spell was cast at. See Rqid: Active Effects for the keys that change an actor or an item. An effect without any changes works as a reminder that the spell is active. The token HUD says which kind an effect is when you hover over it: "Has automated effects" for one with changes, "Only marks the spell while it lasts" for a reminder. If an effect only does part of what the spell does, put the rest in the effect's description, for example "Not automated: −1 strike rank". The HUD shows that line too. You can also edit the effect afterwards from the compendium like any other effect. Unlock the compendium first.
documents.s: 2. Make the effect and give it an rqid

documents.t: Open the spell, and drag the effect from the compendium onto the Spell Effect field. If it doesn't link, the effect has no rqid. Do this for the spell where it is used: the spell on the actor, and the world or compendium spell that new copies come from. That is all for a spell that works on its caster or target. Cast the spell, let the target's owner click Apply, and the effect shows up on the token.

By default an effect goes on the target actor. These two optional settings have no fields on the sheet yet, so set them in the same macro, under system:: system: { changes: [/* … */], // Goes on the target's equipped, non-missile weapon, and asks which one if there are several spellTarget: { documentType: "weapon", where: [ { path: "equippedStatus", op: "eq", value: "equipped" }, { path: "isProjectileWeapon", op: "eq", value: "false" }, ], }, // Can't be on the same weapon as Fireblade incompatibleSpellRqidLinks: [{ rqid: "i.spirit-magic.fireblade" }], }, incompatibleSpellRqidLinks lists spells that can't be on the same target, and cancelsSpellRqidLinks lists opposing spells, like Demoralize and Courage, that cancel each other so that neither remains. supersedesSpellRqidLinks lists spells this one takes precedence over, like Berserker over Fanaticism: casting it removes them, and they have no effect while it's active. counteractsSpellRqidLinks does the same, but only to spells that are weaker, like Harmony against Fanaticism. Strength counts Rune points double and includes boost magic points, and an equal spell isn't weaker. The Bladesharp, Demoralize and Harmony effects in the wiki module are good examples to copy from.
documents.s: Optional: where it goes and what it can't share a target with

documents.t: An effect template can only add an effect to something. A spell that has to do something, like removing other spells, placing a token or healing, needs a small script in a module of your own. The script registers a behavior for the spell's rqid, which runs when Apply is clicked. See Behaviors in the API section.

To change what a spell of the wiki module does, but not how it's cast, make your own version of the spell with the same rqid. A spell is matched to its effect and behavior by rqid, so your copy keeps what the wiki module registered for it. Change the Spell Effect link on your copy to point at your own effect template to replace only the effect. Give yours a higher priority in its rqid editor to make it the best version.

Spells the wiki module doesn't have keep working as before, so there is nothing you must do when upgrading. A world in another language still gets the wiki spells' effects and behaviors, since they are found by rqid, not by name. The effect and the spell don't have to come from the same module. Link a spell in one module to an effect in another by its rqid.

The wiki module contains compendiums with hit locations for most body types including humanoids (see folder Wiki RuneQuest Glorantha / Hit Locations). If you drag a hit location to an actor it will end up in the Combat Tab. The parts of a hit location are:

This is required for identifying the type of this hit location, so that for example armor can be made to cover it. Editing the Rqid can be done by clicking the icon in the window title bar. For more info see the section about Rqid.

When a hitlocation gets damage it will react differently depending on what is selected here. There are four possible values (Limb, Head, Chest & Abdomen). And if Limb is chosen a "Connected To" field is shown. This is to be able to model that an Abdomen that gets a severe hit should make the limbs (legs) useless and the other special handling described in the section "Damage Equal to or More Than the Location’s Hit Points" on page 147-148 in the core rulebook.
This is only shown for Limb hitlocations, see above.
This is the range on the hitlocation D20 roll that this hit location occupies. It is used when determining what hitlocation should get damage.

The armor points added here will reduce damage taken when damage is applied. The total AP of the hitlocation will be this number plus the AP of any equipped armor item that affects this hit location. Active Effects can add to it as well. For example, the Protection spell's effect adds its level to every hit location's natural AP while the spell lasts. See rqid: Active Effects.

The "base location HP" is calculated from the total actor HP, and since different hit locations have different HP the "delta" is used to model how many HP this hit location should have. This value needs to be adjusted for different creature hit locations, but in the wiki there are premade sets of hit locations for different creatures. For special cases that do not follow the general rule, like Gorps that have a single hit location with HP equal to total HP, this field needs to be adjusted on the individual Gorp since the total HP can differ between individuals.

Spirit Magic Spells and Rune Magic Spells are different items, but they cast and take effect the same way. This page explains what they have in common. The two item pages cover what is particular to each: Spirit Magic Spell and Rune Magic Spell.

Cast the spell from the actor sheet. The cast card shows the roll and the magic points or rune points it cost, and one row per target. Each target's protective spells meet it, and if the target can resist the spell, the Resisted By field decides how. When the spell takes effect, the target's owner gets an Apply button on the card. What Apply does depends on what the spell has been given, see below. How a Spell Is Resolved goes through each step in detail: spell areas, wards, Countermagic and Shield, the kinds of resistance, Reflection and Apply. A spell that has been given nothing still works as a cast: the card is posted and the points are spent, but there is no Apply button and the GM and players handle the effect by hand. Spells you add yourself start out like this.

There are two things that make Apply do something, and a spell can have both. An effect template. A spell links to an Active Effect in its Spell Effect field. Apply puts a copy of that effect on the target (or on the target's weapon), named after the spell and its level, like "Bladesharp (3)", and it shows on the token. Most spells in the wiki module work this way. This covers everything an Active Effect can do: change the sheet, or just remind everyone that the spell is active. The effect can also say what the spell can be cast on, and which spells can't share a target with it. A behavior. Some spells need more than an effect on the target, like Dispel Magic, which removes other spells, the elemental summons, which place a token, or Countermagic and Shield, which stop other spells. These are small scripts that a module registers for the spell, which the system runs instead of attaching an effect. The wiki module registers the behaviors for the spells it has. Behaviors are matched on the spell's rqid, so a copy of a spell, in a world or another module, gets the behavior as long as it keeps the rqid. The wiki module ships with both for the spells it covers. For any other spell, for example one from the Red Book of Magic, see Giving your own spells effects.
documents.s: What a spell can be given

documents.t: Field What it does Duration, Range From the rulebook. A Temporal duration is also what Apply gives the effect. Resisted By How a target can resist the spell. A single target resistance roll is automated. Target Kind, Effect Tier What the spell works on and how much of it can be automated. Informational for now. Gets through Countermagic and Shield Check this for spells, like Dismiss Magic, that Countermagic and Shield don't stop. Spell Effect The effect template to apply. Drop an Active Effect with an rqid here, or remove it with the trash can.

A spell cast on a target that already has the same spell active has no effect: the Core Spirit Magic Q&A "Replacing an Existing Spell" (Core p.255) says a recast of a spell still in effect does nothing, so it can't refresh the duration. Variable spells don't add up either (RBM p.5): Protection 1 cast after Protection 2 doesn't make Protection 3. Some spells can't be on the same target together: Bladesharp and Fireblade can't share a weapon, and neither can Protection and Shimmer on a person. The system checks this when Apply is clicked, by the spells' rqids. When a spell has no effect for one of these reasons, Apply says why and the card records it; only the target's owners see the reason. The world setting Recast Spells Take Effect chooses how a recast of the same spell is handled: Never: while the spell is active, a new casting has no effect at any level. This is the Q&A read literally. Only if stronger (default): a casting at a higher level replaces the weaker one, so Protection 1 can be raised to Protection 3 without dispelling it first; an equal or weaker one has no effect. This reads the Q&A as being about refreshing a spell. Always (house rule): every new casting replaces the old one and any incompatible spell, which also refreshes its duration. With Never and Only if stronger, an incompatible spell that is active keeps the new one from taking effect.

Most content from Chaosium's RQG wiki is included in a Foundry VTT module that is a required companion to the main RQG System. The module compendiums are organised into folders: Cults & Magic, including the Spirit Magic Effects and Rune Magic Effects compendiums with the effects spells put on their targets Equipment Bestiary Skills & Passions Runes Occupations & Places Hit Locations Macros & Rolltables In the Bestiary/Adventurers compendium is a "Human (Base)" actor that can be used to build a PC (or NPC). Vasana from the wiki is also in that folder as an example of a more developed character. These and a number of Bestiary creatures are templates, so they can be picked in Foundry's Create Actor dialog, see Creating an Adventurer. danger You will need to have this module active in your world to make the RQG system work since it contains runes etc that is required for various calculations. To begin with only an English language version is provided but hopefully more languages will follow. This is one reason these required compendiums are in a separate module and not in the system itself.
